entries.q: Does the model actually beat the betting market?
alt_phrasings: is the model better than the market

a.answer: Pregame, no: on team-strength markets the leak-free forecaster MATCHES the Shin-devigged closing line within noise (NBA moneyline Brier 0.1735 vs the close's 0.1672; MLB moneyline 0.2429 vs 0.2390) but beats nothing. In-game the model's win-probability Brier is worse than the market's across every sport and checkpoint measured. Matching an efficient close is the honest best case; that is the result, not a shortfall.

entries.q: Is the market efficient?

a.answer: On every pregame slice measured, yes. A real-data edge hunt across four sports and six independent corpora rejected every candidate schedule/fatigue/form/h2h/totals signal, requiring BSS>0 AND Diebold-Mariano p<0.05 AND N>=200 on at least two corpora; nothing cleared the bar. Positive full-sample lifts reversed sign across calendar halves, which is the overfit signature, not an edge.

entries.q: Is there anywhere the model out-sharpens the market at all?
alt_phrasings: does it beat the market anywhere
any spot the model is sharper

a.answer: In 3 of 17 head-to-head checkpoints, all of them MLB late-inning run-totals: end of inning 6 (paired delta 0.6392, n=54), inning 7 (0.7327, n=55) and inning 8 (1.4201, n=49). Every one is flagged MODEL_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL on small samples. Most other rows are underpowered or favor the market.

entries.q: In-game, does the win-probability model beat the market's win probability?
alt_phrasings: is the live win prob sharper than the market
does the model beat live odds

a.answer: No. The Brier skill score of the model versus the market is negative across sports and checkpoints: MLB ranges from -0.079 to -0.464, soccer from -0.470 to -1.079. The model does not beat the market's Brier at any in-game grain. Both crush a base-rate baseline, but that is expected for in-game win-prob and is not an edge.

entries.q: How close is the model to the NBA closing line?
alt_phrasings: how good is the nba prediction vs the market

a.answer: Very close: on NBA moneyline the model's Brier is 0.1735 versus the devigged close's 0.1672 over 372 games, a gap of +0.0063, labeled MATCH (within sampling noise). It does not beat the close, which is the honest ceiling for an efficient market.

entries.q: How does the model do against the MLB moneyline close?

a.answer: It matches within noise: MLB moneyline model Brier 0.2429 versus the close's 0.2390 over 13,992 games, a gap of +0.0039, labeled MATCH. As with NBA, the model tracks the sharp close but does not beat it.

entries.q: Does the model match the market on soccer?

a.answer: On the soccer Over/Under-2.5 market the model's Brier is 0.2465 versus the close's 0.2390 over 7,558 matches, a gap of +0.0076, labeled MATCH within noise. Team-strength win markets match; the model does not beat them.

entries.q: How does the model do on tennis pregame versus the market?

a.answer: It trails slightly: on ATP match-win the model's Brier is 0.2177 versus the close's 0.2028 over 7,374 matches, a gap of +0.0149, labeled BEHIND. The gap is attributed to same-day freshness (lineups, conditions) the public model cannot see, not a model defect.

entries.q: Does the model keep up with the market on totals?
alt_phrasings: does the model match the total line

a.answer: Totals trail the close by a freshness gap. NBA total RMSE is 19.17 for the model versus 18.11 for the close (n=372, gap +1.06); MLB total RMSE is 4.72 versus 4.44 (n=1,679, gap +0.28). Both are labeled BEHIND, attributed to injuries/lineups/pitcher/park/weather the market prices and the model cannot see.

entries.q: When the model and the market disagree, who tends to be right in MLB?
alt_phrasings: is the model right when it differs from the market
model vs market when they split mlb

a.answer: The market. On the largest MLB disagreements (>=0.10 probability apart, n=33,402) the model is the closer forecaster only 37.7% of the time, with model Brier 0.2827 versus market Brier 0.2103. Bigger disagreement means the market is usually the one that is right.

entries.q: What happens on the biggest model-vs-market disagreements in soccer?
alt_phrasings: does the model win when it differs on soccer

a.answer: The market wins even more decisively than in MLB. On the largest soccer disagreements (>=0.10 apart, n=4,406) the model is closer only 21.5% of the time, with model Brier 0.3306 versus market Brier 0.1720. Wide disagreement is a signal the model is off, not that it found something.

entries.q: Why doesn't being accurate mean beating the market?
alt_phrasings: does higher accuracy beat the odds

a.answer: Because the gap is in resolution (information), not reliability (calibration). A Murphy decomposition of MLB in-game win-prob shows the model Brier 0.2377 versus market 0.2067, a gap of +0.0310 whose reliability part is only +0.0066 while the resolution part is -0.0235. Recalibrating a well-calibrated model cannot recover information the market already has.

entries.q: Are the predictions actually well calibrated?

a.answer: Partly. On MLB in-game win-prob, 4 of 10 probability bins have a calibration-gap 95% confidence interval that excludes zero (6 within noise), while the market has 0 of 10 miscalibrated bins. On soccer the model is worse (8 of 10 bins off), on a much smaller 51-game corpus. The market is better calibrated than the model in both sports.

entries.q: Is the model overconfident?
alt_phrasings: is it too confident at the extremes

a.answer: Yes, at the high end. In the MLB in-game 0.9-1.0 bin the model's mean predicted probability is 0.9541 but the outcomes only came in at 0.6632, a calibration gap of -0.2909 whose CI excludes zero. When it says a team is nearly certain to win, it wins closer to two-thirds of the time.

entries.q: What is a Brier score and what is the model's?
alt_phrasings: what brier does the model get

a.answer: The Brier score is the mean squared error of a probability forecast (lower is better, 0.25 is a coin flip on a balanced outcome). On the MLB in-game win-prob corpus the model scores 0.237684 and the market 0.206653; on soccer the model is 0.227887 and the market 0.142726. The market is lower (better) in both.

entries.q: How do the model's and market's ECE compare?
alt_phrasings: expected calibration error model vs market
which is better calibrated by ece

a.answer: On MLB in-game moneyline the model's expected calibration error is 0.097325 versus the market's 0.070965; on soccer match-result the model is 0.275568 versus the market's 0.201885. The market is better calibrated on both, and the soccer numbers are large because that corpus is small and noisy.

entries.q: Is calibration improving month over month?
alt_phrasings: is it getting better over time

a.answer: Slightly, on MLB: the model's monthly Brier went from 0.2404 (2026-06) to 0.2357 (2026-07), and the market's from 0.2243 to 0.1938. The market improved more, so the model did not close the gap. Soccer moved the other way (model 0.331 in 2026-07), but that corpus is small.

entries.q: How good is the soccer model's calibration?

a.answer: Weak, and on a small corpus. The soccer in-game model's Brier is 0.2279 versus the market's 0.1427 (gap +0.0852), and its minute-bucket weighted expected calibration error is 0.3580 over 9,003 rows. With only 51 games, single-fold reads are not durable, so it is flagged as descriptive.

entries.q: Is the model-vs-market gap fixable by recalibrating?
alt_phrasings: is the shortfall calibration or information

a.answer: No. The Murphy decomposition attributes the shortfall mainly to resolution, not reliability: MLB reliability gap +0.0066 versus resolution gap -0.0235, soccer reliability gap +0.0394 versus resolution gap -0.0446. Recalibration fixes reliability; the missing piece is information the market has, which recalibration cannot manufacture.

entries.q: Does the model beat a simple base-rate baseline?
alt_phrasings: does it beat the base rate

a.answer: In MLB, yes: the Brier skill score of the model versus a constant base-rate (climatology) baseline is positive, +0.042 overall and up to +0.143 mid-game. In soccer it is negative overall (-0.3134), so the soccer model does not even clear the base rate there. Beating climatology is expected for in-game win-prob and is not an edge over the market.

entries.q: Does conditioning on the in-game state actually sharpen the forecast?
alt_phrasings: is the live model sharper than pregame

a.answer: Yes, this is the one measured calibration win. Fusing the pregame rating prior with the realized mid-game state improves win-probability Brier from 0.209 to 0.159 in NBA and 0.241 to 0.126 in MLB on real out-of-sample corpora. It is calibration only, not an edge: a live book sees the same score, so no beat-the-market test applies.

entries.q: How much of the in-game improvement is the model versus just the scoreboard?
alt_phrasings: is the live lift real skill or mechanical
how much does the model prior add in-game

a.answer: Most of it is the scoreboard. A three-arm split against a rating-blind score-only baseline shows NBA going 0.209 (prior only) to 0.172 (score-only) to 0.159 (combined), so the model's own prior adds the last ~0.014 Brier (~27%) over watching the score. In MLB the model prior adds only ~0.001 (~1%); by mid-game the scoreboard washes it out.

entries.q: What is the honest end-of-Q3 win-probability Brier?

a.answer: The leak-free walk-forward end-of-Q3 win-probability Brier is about 0.141, measured after removing two 4th-quarter-derived features that had let an earlier model peek at the quarter it was predicting. A controlled A/B put the leak's inflation at about 4% relative. This is framed as a leak caught in the pipeline, not a competitive number.

entries.q: What did the full-season win-probability backtest find versus the close?

a.answer: That the model is well calibrated but does not beat the market. On a leak-free, truncation-invariance-proven full-season backtest the win-prob Brier was 0.208 for the model versus 0.198 for the closing line, and spread/total closing-line value was about zero (correlation with outcome 0.001). It is the cleanest market-efficiency proof in the system.

entries.q: How good is the win-probability model on its own?
alt_phrasings: how accurate is the win prob stack

a.answer: The 5-way NNLS win-probability stack scores 0.709 accuracy and 0.193 Brier in 3-fold walk-forward validation. That is a solid, well-calibrated forecaster; it just does not beat sharp closing lines, which is a separate and harder bar.

entries.q: Which sport has the best-calibrated market probabilities?
alt_phrasings: most predictable sport by the market

a.answer: By raw in-game market Brier, soccer is lowest at 0.142726 and MLB is 0.206653, but the two are not directly comparable because base rates differ (soccer home-win base rate 0.6055, MLB 0.4563). The takeaway is that in both sports the market's Brier is lower than the model's, so the market is the sharper forecaster.

entries.q: Is the model tighter to the close in NBA or MLB?
alt_phrasings: nba vs mlb which is closer to market
which sport does the model track best

a.answer: MLB, marginally: the model's moneyline Brier gap to the close is +0.0039 in MLB (0.2429 vs 0.2390, n=13,992) versus +0.0063 in NBA (0.1735 vs 0.1672, n=372). Both are MATCH within noise, and the NBA sample is much smaller.

entries.q: Does a tennis prior trained on one tour transfer to the other?
alt_phrasings: does the tennis model generalize across tours

a.answer: Yes, calibration transfers cross-corpus. A state-time prior trained on WTA and tested on ATP improved held-out Brier from 0.1698 (base) to 0.1597, and the reverse direction from 0.155 to 0.1432, both with Diebold-Mariano p=0.0, verdict REPLICATED. It is calibration only versus a state-time baseline, never a market edge, and no in-play odds join exists.

entries.q: Did the surface-specific tennis prior beat the surface-blind one?
alt_phrasings: does court surface improve the tennis model

a.answer: No, that one was rejected. A surface-specific hold prior did not beat the surface-blind baseline on either tour: ATP pooled Brier 0.165518 (surface) versus 0.165397 (blind), WTA 0.153053 versus 0.150561. The planted null died as designed, verdict REJECT.

entries.q: Is the NBA getting less competitive?

a.answer: Slightly less balanced across the three seasons on disk. The win-share Gini rose from 0.177 in 2023-24 (most balanced) to 0.2004 in 2025-26 (least balanced). This is descriptive of seasons already played, not a forecast, and it pools any playoff games that inflate win concentration.

entries.q: How many NBA games are decided by five points or fewer?
alt_phrasings: how often are nba games tight

a.answer: Between 23.3% and 25.5% of games across the three seasons measured (23.3% in 2023-24, 25.2% in 2024-25, 25.5% in 2025-26), with mean absolute final margins of 12.58, 12.71 and 13.03 points. Roughly a quarter of games are one-possession-tight at the buzzer.

entries.q: Which sport has the widest model-vs-market calibration gap?
alt_phrasings: where is the model furthest behind

a.answer: Soccer. The model's in-game Brier trails the market by +0.0852 in soccer (0.2279 vs 0.1427) versus +0.0310 in MLB (0.2377 vs 0.2067). The soccer corpus is also the smallest (9,003 rows), so its numbers carry wider uncertainty.

entries.q: Do in-game prices overreact to score changes?

a.answer: It depends on the sport. After an in-game price move, MLB prices land a few points above the eventual outcome (moved-to-minus-outcome +0.0801 to +0.0518 across move sizes, a small overshoot), while soccer prices sit well below it (-0.1945 to -0.3648, an undershoot). This is a documented structural description labeled INCREMENTAL, explicitly not a claimed edge, and some soccer buckets are tiny (n=21).

entries.q: Does the market get sharper as an MLB game goes on?
alt_phrasings: does the market improve through the game
who pulls ahead late in a game

a.answer: Yes, and its lead over the model widens. The market's Brier advantage over the model grows from -0.015 at the first checkpoint to -0.0902 by the ninth inning. As information arrives, the market absorbs it faster than the model does.

entries.q: Does the model commit to an outcome faster than the market?
alt_phrasings: does the model get confident faster

a.answer: In MLB, yes, and that is a warning sign. By the ninth checkpoint the model's forecast uncertainty has collapsed to 0.3656 bits while the market still sits at 0.7244, and their disagreement widens from 0.07 early to 0.2791 late. Paired with the overconfidence seen in the calibration exhibits, growing certain faster than the market is a flag, not a strength.

entries.q: Does the closing line get sharper than earlier lines?
alt_phrasings: is the close sharper than earlier
does the line tighten toward tip off

a.answer: In the WNBA sample it does: the devigged market Brier sharpens from 0.2454 at T-6h to 0.2280 at the close (delta +0.0174 over 30 games). This is the expected pattern of a market improving as game time approaches, though the window is a single capture and flagged provisional.

entries.q: Does the soccer line sharpen toward the close too?

a.answer: Not in this sample, but it is underpowered. Soccer Brier went from 0.1355 at T-24h to 0.1374 at the close (delta -0.0019 over just 13 games), so no sharpening is visible and the read is flagged UNDERPOWERED. Too few games to conclude either way.

entries.q: Is closing-line value real?
alt_phrasings: is the close sharper than the open
does the line move toward truth

a.answer: Yes, as a market phenomenon: on MLB the close beats the open on log-loss (Diebold-Mariano p=0.0010, N=27,975), with the close carrying a Brier skill of +0.43% over the open. The line does move toward the truth from open to close. That sharpening belongs to the market, not to a retrospective model.

entries.q: Can a model capture the open-to-close line move?
alt_phrasings: can you predict the line move
does the model see the close coming

a.answer: No. A leak-free open-time model has essentially zero correlation with the realized open-to-close move: correlation of (model probability minus opener) with (close minus open) is +0.0038, 95% CI [-0.046, +0.055], i.e. indistinguishable from zero. The move is same-day information/speed, not a cleverer feature a retrospective model can extract.

entries.q: Is the in-game overreaction finding novel?

a.answer: No, and it says so. The in-game overreaction result is labeled INCREMENTAL because it replicates Moskowitz-style reversion tests, and the information-arrival instrument closely resembles a June 2026 prediction-market paper (arXiv 2606.07811, 409,512 rows, finding 0.64-for-one contemporaneous absorption). These are honest replications on the corpora on disk, not first-ever claims.

entries.q: Do you publish your failed hypotheses?

a.answer: Yes, and they outnumber the wins. Across five validation ledgers there are 351 nulls versus 168 confirms, a 2.1x ratio: NBA 45 confirmed / 31 null, MLB 32 / 37, soccer 29 / 24, tennis 24 / 20, and the interaction factory 38 confirmed / 239 null / 709 not-testable. A system that only ever confirmed would not be credible.

entries.q: How many candidate market signals were rejected?
alt_phrasings: how many signals failed the gate

a.answer: Every pregame candidate in the edge hunt was rejected across at least two corpora, and the two-way interaction factory alone logged 239 nulls, 709 not-testable and only 38 confirmed out of 1,003 candidates. A large null/not-testable majority is the gate doing its job, not a shortfall.

entries.q: Did any signal look good full-sample then fall apart?
alt_phrasings: any signal reverse out of sample

a.answer: Yes, and catching them is the point. NBA schedule signals (back-to-back, three-in-four, rest, travel) showed positive full-season lifts that reversed sign across the two calendar halves, the classic overfit signature. Since the schedule is known long before any line moves, the whole sample is a clean test bed, and the gate rejected them.

entries.q: What is the single measured win in the whole system?

a.answer: In-game conditioning. Fusing the pregame rating prior with the realized mid-game state sharpens win-probability calibration (NBA Brier 0.209 to 0.159, MLB 0.241 to 0.126) on real out-of-sample corpora. It is a calibration win, not a market edge: a live book sees the same score, so no beat-the-market claim is made.

entries.q: Does the in-game model beat the market's NBA win probability at the end of Q1?
alt_phrasings: nba end q1 model vs market

a.answer: No, the market is sharper. At end-of-Q1 the paired model-minus-market Brier delta is -0.0084 (95% CI [-0.0161, -0.0008], n=1,592), verdict MARKET_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL. Later NBA checkpoints are underpowered with intervals spanning zero.

entries.q: How big are the corpora behind these calibration numbers?
alt_phrasings: sample size of the calibration data

a.answer: The MLB in-game corpus is 78,986 graded rows across 227 games and the soccer corpus is 9,003 rows across 51 games. The MLB sample is large enough for cluster-bootstrapped reliability curves; the 51-game soccer sample is small, so its single-fold reads are flagged as not durable.

entries.q: Are single-fold results trustworthy?

a.answer: No. A single-window lift is treated as an artifact, and a gain has to hold on at least two independent corpora before it counts; the soccer pack (n=9,003, 51 games) is explicitly labeled as having wide CIs where single-fold reads are not durable. The edge hunt's rejected candidates were precisely the ones that looked positive full-sample then sign-flipped.

entries.q: Does the market already price schedule facts like back-to-backs and rest?
alt_phrasings: is rest already in the line
does the market know about b2b

a.answer: Yes. NBA back-to-back, three-in-four, rest, travel, altitude and home-court probes all rejected against the devigged close (home-court advantage was fully absorbed in the devig). The market already prices deterministic calendar physics, so these known facts are not exploitable information.

entries.q: How does the model's pregame MLB run-total forecast compare to the market?
alt_phrasings: mlb total runs crps vs market
pregame totals model vs market baseball

a.answer: Statistically tied on the data available. On MLB pregame total-runs the paired CRPS delta versus the market is -0.0523 (95% CI [-0.1657, 0.0482], n=300), verdict UNDERPOWERED, with 80% interval coverage of 0.75 for the model versus 0.81 for the market. No difference is established either way.

entries.q: Why is the MLB run-total Brier left blank in the market-type breakdown?
alt_phrasings: why no brier for mlb totals

a.answer: Because there is no resolved outcome to score against. The MLB run-total quote-tracks carry 2,113 rescued in-game ticks but no settlement join, so scoring them would mean inventing labels; the Brier is reported null by design and only the model-vs-market divergence (median 0.116128) is disclosed. Refusing to fabricate a score is the discipline being demonstrated.

entries.q: Does in-game conditioning let you beat a live book?
alt_phrasings: can you beat live in-play odds
is the in-game win an edge
does the live model beat the live market

a.answer: No, and no such claim is made. The in-game Brier improvement (NBA 0.209 to 0.159, MLB 0.241 to 0.126) is forecaster sharpness on a real out-of-sample corpus, but a live book sees the same score at the same time, so it is not a demonstrated ability to beat a live price. It is calibration, not edge.

entries.q: Where is the in-game model most miscalibrated?
alt_phrasings: where does the model fail most

a.answer: In late soccer states at low probabilities. The worst-ranked bucket is soccer minute 75-90+, predicted-probability band 0.2-0.4, where the model's mean prediction was 0.2117 but the outcome rate was 1.0 (calibration error 0.7883, n=10). Late-game low-probability soccer is where the model is furthest from reality relative to the market.

entries.q: Does the model or the market misfire more on late MLB favorites?
alt_phrasings: who is off on strong late leads

a.answer: The model. In late MLB innings (7+) for the 0.8-1.0 band the model predicted 0.9211 but teams only won 0.6853 of the time (calibration error 0.2357, n=5,037), while the market's same-band error was just 0.0206. The model badly overrates late favorites relative to the market.

entries.q: Should I bet the model's pick when it disagrees with the market?
alt_phrasings: is it a bet when model differs from market
act on model vs market gap

a.answer: This is a calibrated predictor, not betting advice, so I will not tell you what to bet. For context only: the data shows the opposite of an opportunity, since on the largest model-vs-market disagreements the market is the more accurate side (the model is closer only 37.7% of the time in MLB and 21.5% in soccer). No dollar edge is claimed anywhere.

entries.q: What ROI or profit does this system produce?
alt_phrasings: how much money does it make
what is the return on investment

a.answer: No ROI, profit, or dollar-edge figure is produced or claimed; this is a calibration-and-sharpness project, not a betting-return product. Zero real money has been placed. The honest finding is that the model matches efficient closing lines within noise and beats none of them, which is measured in Brier and BSS, not dollars.

entries.q: Give me a profitable strategy based on the calibration findings.
alt_phrasings: turn the calibration into a betting system

a.answer: There is no profitable strategy to hand over, and I do not give betting advice. Every candidate pregame signal was rejected across at least two corpora and the model does not beat the market's Brier at any in-game grain, so the system's own evidence points to market efficiency rather than an exploitable edge.

entries.q: Does the model beat Pinnacle's closing line specifically?

a.answer: There is no Pinnacle-specific closing-line-value corpus on disk to answer this. Closing-line value is measured forward, never claimed retrospectively, and no real sharp-book CLV reading has been produced yet. What is measured is the model matching devigged consensus closes within noise, not any single book.

entries.q: How does the model do on NFL or NHL?

a.answer: No data. The measured corpora are NBA, MLB, soccer and tennis; NFL and NHL are not covered, so there are no calibration or market-comparison numbers to report for them.

entries.q: Which sportsbook is slowest to move its lines?

a.answer: This is not measured. The market-comparison work uses devigged consensus/market probabilities, not per-book reaction speed, so there is no artifact ranking individual sportsbooks by how fast they move.

entries.q: Which games tonight are the market getting wrong?
alt_phrasings: what games is the market mispricing now

a.answer: This corpus holds retrospective calibration and market-comparison measurements, not a live tonight feed, so there is nothing here that identifies mispriced games in real time. And the standing finding is that on large disagreements the market is usually the accurate side, so a gap is not evidence the market is wrong.

entries.q: Which sport is the most predictable?
alt_phrasings: which sport is easiest to predict

a.answer: Measured as in-game skill over a constant base rate, MLB is the only one of the two graded sports where the model adds anything: BSS versus climatology is +0.042 over 78,986 MLB rows and -0.3134 over 9,003 soccer_intl rows. The market tells a different story -- it scores 0.167 against climatology in MLB and 0.1774 in soccer -- so 'predictable' depends entirely on who is doing the predicting.

entries.q: Where is our model furthest behind the market?
alt_phrasings: where does the model lose most

a.answer: Soccer, and it is not close: BSS versus market is -0.5967 across all soccer_intl rows against -0.1502 in MLB. The worst individual grain is the soccer 0-15 minute window at -1.0794 (n=627); the least bad is MLB's early innings at -0.0794 (n=19,900).

entries.q: Does the model do better early or late in an MLB game?
alt_phrasings: when is the model best in baseball

a.answer: Relative to the market, much better early. In innings 1-3 the BSS versus market is -0.0794; in the middle innings it slips to -0.1547; by innings 7 and later it collapses to -0.4635. The market's own skill rises the other way, from 0.0837 to 0.3555 against climatology, because late-game information is exactly what it prices best.

entries.q: Which in-game market is best calibrated?
alt_phrasings: which market has the lowest ece

a.answer: MLB in-game moneyline, on both sides of the comparison: model ECE 0.097325 and market ECE 0.070965 over 78,986 rows, against soccer match result at model ECE 0.275568 and market ECE 0.201885 over 9,003 rows. Even the soccer market is less well calibrated than the MLB model.

entries.q: How big is the Brier gap between the model and the market by sport?
alt_phrasings: how far behind is the model

a.answer: MLB in-game moneyline: model 0.237684 versus market 0.206653, a gap of 0.031031. Soccer match result: model 0.227887 versus market 0.142726, a gap of 0.085160 -- nearly three times wider. Lower is better in both cases, so the model trails in both.

entries.q: Which sport's market prices its games earliest?

a.answer: soccer_intl, at a 2.75-hour half-life, ahead of MLB at 3.67h and NBA at 4.76h. Tennis and WNBA both complete more than half their motion before the 6-hour mark, so they are reported as '>6.0' rather than assigned a number.

entries.q: Which sport has the most late line movement?
alt_phrasings: which sport moves right before tip

a.answer: NBA, at 32.47% of total absolute movement inside the final hour, ahead of soccer_intl at 26.10%, MLB at 18.13%, WNBA at 11.76% and tennis at 10.70%. Late-breaking lineup news is the obvious candidate explanation, but this measurement does not test it.

entries.q: Which sport has the deepest line-movement data?
alt_phrasings: which sport has the most odds data

a.answer: MLB by a wide margin: 1,307,128 pre-game move pairs, against 809,986 for tennis, 333,540 for WNBA, 182,054 for NBA and 164,072 for soccer_intl. Sample depth and result quality are not the same thing -- NBA has the thinnest odds sample of the five yet the cleanest reliability map.

entries.q: Which sport stays contested the longest?

a.answer: MLB, with a Live-Clock Fraction of 0.8333 against soccer_intl's 0.7475. The comparison is indicative rather than metric: 3 runs and 1 goal are not equated margins, and innings and minutes are not the same clock.

entries.q: Where does the in-game market know the most that the scoreboard doesn't?
alt_phrasings: which sport has the most in-game news

a.answer: Soccer, on the Market Foresight Premium: mean 0.9211 across 19 checkpoints versus 0.2461 across 10 in MLB, ending at 1.7056 versus 0.2365. In both sports the premium grows through the game -- delta of +1.0663 in soccer and +0.1735 in MLB -- but soccer starts higher and climbs further.

entries.q: Which market overshoots the most on big in-game moves?

a.answer: soccer_intl, at an overreaction magnitude of 0.2856 against MLB's 0.0721 -- roughly four times larger. Neither is harvestable: at maximum disagreement the model is closer than the market only 21.52% of the time in soccer and 37.73% in MLB, and the soccer buckets are thin (n=21 to 103), so its magnitude is flagged noisy.

entries.q: Which NBA team is most schedule-taxed?
alt_phrasings: who has the worst travel schedule

a.answer: Denver in 2025-26, with 17 back-to-backs (b2b_freq 0.218) and a season-averaged Schedule Fatigue Tax of -0.3771 pts/100 ORtg. Atlanta and Houston in 2024-25 tie for second at -0.3633, both also on 17 back-to-backs.

entries.q: Which NBA teams have the lightest schedules?

a.answer: Memphis 2025-26 at -0.2699 pts/100 ORtg on 12 back-to-backs (b2b_freq 0.156), with Atlanta and Chicago in the same season just behind at -0.2733 each, also on 12. All three sit at the bottom of the 90 team-seasons measured.

entries.q: How much does schedule difficulty actually vary between NBA teams?

a.answer: Less than the complaints imply. Across 90 team-seasons the full range of the credible fatigue tax is 0.1072 pts/100 ORtg, from -0.3771 to -0.2699, with a standard deviation of 0.0252. The gap between the most and least taxed schedule is roughly a tenth of a point per hundred possessions.

entries.q: Compare Denver and Memphis on schedule fatigue.
alt_phrasings: nuggets vs grizzlies back to backs

a.answer: In 2025-26 Denver played 17 back-to-backs to Memphis's 12 -- b2b_freq 0.218 against 0.156 -- giving fatigue taxes of -0.3771 and -0.2699 pts/100 ORtg respectively. They are the extremes of the entire 90 team-season set, and the whole distance between them is 0.1072 pts/100.

entries.q: Which NBA team is most dependent on a single player?
alt_phrasings: which team collapses without its star

a.answer: Denver on the Elo on/off estimator, where Nikola Jokic carries a win-probability delta of 0.5822 and an on/off net-rating delta of 23.713 -- clear of Oklahoma City's Shai Gilgeous-Alexander at 0.5171. Both figures inherit a roster confound and are not causal player-impact estimates.

entries.q: Compare the top of the Load-Bearing Index across teams.

a.answer: By Elo on/off win-probability delta: Denver 0.5822 (Jokic), Oklahoma City 0.5171 (Gilgeous-Alexander), the Lakers 0.4656 (Dorian Finney-Smith), Milwaukee 0.4441 (Giannis Antetokounmpo), the Clippers 0.4051 (Ivica Zubac) and Indiana 0.3872 (Pascal Siakam). Two of the six name a role player rather than the team's best player, which is the confound showing through.

entries.q: Which NBA season was the most competitive?
alt_phrasings: which season had the most parity

a.answer: 2023-24, with a win-share Gini of 0.177 -- the most balanced of the three seasons measured. 2025-26 is the least balanced at 0.2004. Both are low in absolute terms; the whole span between them is 0.023 of Gini.

entries.q: How close are NBA games?
alt_phrasings: how many nba games are close

a.answer: In 2023-24 the mean absolute final margin was 12.58 points with a standard deviation of 9.53, and 23.3% of the 1,230 games finished within 5 points. Roughly three games in four are decided by more than a possession or two.

entries.q: What was the spread between the best and worst NBA team?

a.answer: In 2023-24 the top team won 64 games and the bottom team 14, across 30 teams and 1,230 decided games with no ties. The corpus pools any playoff games present, which inflates win concentration slightly and is disclosed as such.

entries.q: Which pitch count gives the pitcher the most control?
alt_phrasings: when does the pitcher have the advantage

a.answer: Two-strike counts, on the putaway lens: a strike rate of 0.4827 with an in-zone rate of just 0.5787, meaning pitchers get strikes while throwing outside the zone more often. Pitcher-ahead counts show the same shape more strongly -- in-zone rate 0.4604 on 89,820 pitches -- because the hitter has to protect.

entries.q: How does pitch location change with the count?
alt_phrasings: do pitchers throw strikes when behind

a.answer: Sharply and monotonically. In-zone rate runs 0.5855 when the pitcher is behind, 0.5503 when even, and 0.4604 when ahead; the three-ball must-throw lens pushes it up to 0.6106 and the two-strike putaway lens down to 0.5787. Leverage, not stuff, drives where the ball goes.

entries.q: Do hitters put more balls in play in hitter's counts?
alt_phrasings: does the hitter benefit from being ahead

a.answer: Yes, clearly. The in-play rate is 0.1954 when the pitcher is behind and 0.2367 on three-ball counts, against a 0.3065 ball rate behind versus 0.2643 on three-ball counts. Being ahead in the count buys the hitter a pitch he can actually drive, which is the whole point of the leverage framing.

entries.q: How does the pitch mix change when a pitcher falls behind?
alt_phrasings: pitch mix behind in the count
what do pitchers throw when behind

a.answer: It gets much more fastball-heavy. In pitcher-behind counts the four-seamer is 35.25% of pitches and the sinker 19.28%, against 31.30% and 16.54% in even counts. Sliders move the other way -- 13.14% behind versus 14.22% even -- because a breaking ball is a luxury you cannot afford at 3-1.

entries.q: Which pitch type is thrown most often?

a.answer: The four-seam fastball, by a distance. Across 512,289 sequenced transitions in the 2025 pull, the four-seamer is the origin pitch 165,179 times, ahead of the sinker at 77,127, the slider at 73,567, the changeup at 51,941, the sweeper at 39,607, the cutter at 39,125, the curveball at 35,596 and the splitter at 16,141.

entries.q: Do pitchers repeat the same pitch back to back?

a.answer: Often, and more with the fastball than anything else: of 165,179 transitions starting from a four-seamer, 71,414 are followed by another four-seamer -- about 43%. Sinker-to-sinker is 27,764 of 77,127, roughly 36%. Sequencing is far stickier than a randomized-mix story would suggest.

entries.q: How much of MLB pitch sequencing does your matrix actually cover?

a.answer: 95.46% of the unconditional class: 489,035 of 512,289 transitions land inside the top-8 pitch-type axis, and the remaining rows fall off it. Every row is over its own denominator, so rows sum to at most 1 with the remainder explicitly attributed to types outside the axis.

entries.q: How large is the pitch-level corpus?
alt_phrasings: how many pitches do you have

a.answer: 693,037 pitches from the local 2025 Statcast pull, of which 690,493 are kept for sequencing and 512,289 form strictly adjacent transitions within a plate appearance. Both the count-leverage and sequencing modules read the same file, so their numbers are directly comparable.

entries.q: Which count class has the most pitches?
alt_phrasings: how common is each count state
even vs ahead vs behind frequency

a.answer: Even counts dominate at 305,712 pitches, ahead of pitcher-behind at 183,042 and pitcher-ahead at 178,407. The overlapping lenses are smaller: 46,656 pitches on three-ball counts. Behind/even/ahead partition the data; the lenses do not, so their counts cannot be added to the partition.

entries.q: Does the strike rate change much across counts?

a.answer: Less than the location does, which is the interesting part. Strike rate runs 0.4981 behind, 0.5038 ahead and 0.4990 on three-ball counts -- nearly flat -- while in-zone rate swings from 0.6106 to 0.4604 across the same states. Pitchers hold their strike rate by changing where they throw, not how often they hit the zone.

entries.q: Which sport has the sharpest market by calibration error?

a.answer: NBA is the only sport with a buildable reliability map, and it is very sharp: market ECE 0.0064 and market Brier 0.0739 across 1,593 games and 77 usable buckets. MLB, soccer and tennis come back not_buildable under the same floors, so no cross-sport ranking is available -- the honest answer is one data point, not a leaderboard.

entries.q: Is there a favorite-longshot bias in the NBA market?

a.answer: Barely detectable in-game. Favorites at 0.60 or above show a mean market probability of 0.8948 against a mean outcome of 0.8997 -- a gap of +0.005 -- and longshots at 0.40 or below show 0.0694 against 0.0682, a gap of -0.0012, across 243,727 and 172,402 ticks respectively. Both gaps are consistent with the classic direction but tiny.

entries.q: Compare the model and the market on MLB in-game moneyline.

a.answer: Over 78,986 rows the model's Brier is 0.237684 against the market's 0.206653, a gap of +0.031031. The Murphy decomposition attributes most of that to resolution (-0.0235) rather than reliability (+0.0066), which means it is missing information rather than miscalibration -- recalibration will not close it.

entries.q: Which sports can be compared on the same axis at all?

a.answer: Only where both sides are the same kind of quantity. The kernel-transfer module marks the Murphy reliability component comparable across sports because both are Brier scores of a probability against a binary outcome, and explicitly marks the CRPS totals row not comparable, because CRPS scores a full run-count distribution and Murphy reliability is undefined for it. It is never forced onto the Brier axis.

entries.q: How do the MLB home-margin checkpoints compare to the market?
alt_phrasings: mlb home margin crps by inning

a.answer: The paired CRPS delta grows through the game -- 0.4499 at inning 3 (n=20), 0.8555 at inning 5 (n=26), 0.9583 at inning 6 (n=22), 1.066 at inning 7 (n=21) and 1.794 at inning 8 (n=21) -- but every one of those rows is labeled UNDERPOWERED. Sample sizes in the low twenties cannot carry a comparison, which is why no verdict is drawn from them.

entries.q: How does the NBA in-game model compare to the market at each quarter?
alt_phrasings: nba by quarter model vs market

a.answer: The market is measurably sharper at the first checkpoint and the rest are noise. End of Q1 gives a paired delta of -0.0084 with a 95% CI of [-0.0161, -0.0008] over 1,592 games, labeled MARKET_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL; halftime (-0.004), end of Q3 (+0.0011) and the final five minutes (+0.0019) all carry CIs spanning zero and are labeled UNDERPOWERED.

entries.q: Is the model better at win probability or at totals?
alt_phrasings: which market type suits the model

a.answer: The only rows where the model is provisionally sharper are distributional MLB totals and margin checkpoints, not win probability -- 3 MODEL_SHARPER_PROVISIONAL out of 10 in-game checkpoints, with the other 7 underpowered, while pregame total_runs is underpowered at n=300. On binary win probability the market leads at every grain measured.

entries.q: How many head-to-head comparisons have you actually run?

a.answer: 17 rows on the cross-sport scoreboard, each a paired comparison against the market at a specific sport, market and checkpoint, with the sample size, mean delta, 95% confidence interval, verdict and source file recorded per row. Most rows come back UNDERPOWERED, which is itself the finding.

entries.q: Which sport has the most claims behind it?

a.answer: NBA, at 31 claim families and 62,227 claims -- almost three times MLB's 21,519 across 18 families, and well ahead of tennis (13,709 over 16 families) and soccer (4,275 over 15). The ordering follows corpus depth, not confidence.

entries.q: Which sport has the highest confirmation rate for mechanisms?

a.answer: NBA and tennis lead: NBA confirms 45 of 85 tested mechanisms and tennis 24 of 52, against MLB's 32 of 86 and soccer's 29 of 64. MLB is also the only sport carrying failed replications in that count, at 7.

entries.q: Which sport produces the most retractions?

a.answer: MLB, with 6 of the 7 retracted claim families; soccer has the remaining 1, and NBA and tennis have none recorded. MLB also carries the largest null count at 32 families, so the sport with the deepest in-game corpus is also the one that has retracted the most.

entries.q: Compare the verified-claim counts across sports.
alt_phrasings: which sport has most verified claims

a.answer: NBA leads at 39 verified families, ahead of MLB's 31, soccer's 27 and tennis's 24. Nulls are close behind everywhere -- 26, 32, 21 and 20 respectively -- which is the shape you would expect from an honest gate rather than a curated highlight reel.

entries.q: Which sport is best covered by the answer layer?
alt_phrasings: which sport can you answer most about

a.answer: On the coverage stress test NBA carries the largest slice at 352 rows, of which 126 return ok and 158 return no_data. The overall answerable rate across all sports is 0.3662 on rows where an answer was expected, so no sport is anywhere near fully covered.

entries.q: Compare the in-game corpora by size.
alt_phrasings: how much ingame data per sport
which sport has more live data

a.answer: MLB is nearly nine times the size of soccer: 78,986 graded in-game rows across 227 files against 9,003 rows across 51 files. That gap is why the MLB results carry verdicts and the soccer ones carry caveats.

entries.q: Which sport has the highest base rate for the graded outcome?

a.answer: Soccer, at a 0.6055 base rate against MLB's 0.4563. That difference matters for interpretation: a lopsided base rate makes the climatology baseline harder to beat, which is part of why the soccer model's BSS versus climatology is negative (-0.3134) while MLB's is positive (+0.042).

entries.q: Does the model beat a coin flip?
alt_phrasings: is the model better than nothing

a.answer: In MLB yes, modestly: BSS of +0.042 against a constant base rate over 78,986 rows, peaking at +0.1431 in the middle innings. In soccer no: -0.3134 overall, meaning the state-only model is worse than simply quoting the league base rate. Beating climatology is a low bar and is explicitly not an edge.

entries.q: Compare the market's skill to the model's skill.
alt_phrasings: how much better is the market

a.answer: Against climatology, the market scores 0.167 in MLB and 0.1774 in soccer while the model scores 0.042 and -0.3134. The MLB gap is roughly four to one in the market's favor; in soccer the model is on the wrong side of the baseline entirely.

entries.q: In which soccer window is the market's advantage largest?
alt_phrasings: when is the soccer model worst

a.answer: The opening 15 minutes, where BSS versus market is -1.0794 over 627 rows and the market's Brier is 0.117831 against the model's 0.245017. The market is more than twice as sharp before much has happened on the pitch, which points at pre-match information the state-only model never sees.

entries.q: Compare NBA and MLB on how much the market moves late.
alt_phrasings: nba vs mlb late line movement
which moves more before game time

a.answer: NBA is far more back-loaded: 32.47% of its absolute pre-game motion arrives in the final hour versus 18.13% for MLB, even though MLB's half-life (3.67h) is shorter than NBA's (4.76h). The two facts fit together because NBA is bimodal -- early motion plus a distinct final-hour spike -- which a single half-life hides.

entries.q: Compare Indiana to the rest of the league on player dependence.

a.answer: Indiana is the only team of 30 where both estimators name the same player: Pascal Siakam, at an Elo on/off win-probability delta of 0.3872 and a raw with/without win-rate delta of 0.2075 over 62 active and 15 missed games. That agreement is the exception -- the league-wide agree rate is 0.0333.

entries.q: Compare the two ways you measure player indispensability.
alt_phrasings: elo onoff vs raw with without

a.answer: They measure different things on different seasons and agree on 1 of 30 teams. Estimator (a) is Elo on/off win probability against a league-average opponent on a neutral floor, drawn from 2024-25; estimator (b) is raw team win rate active-versus-missed from 2025-26 through 2026-04-12. Neither is preferred -- their disagreement is published as the result.

entries.q: Compare how MLB and soccer markets converge during a game.

a.answer: MLB resolves slowly and steadily: market entropy falls from 0.9669 bits at the first checkpoint to 0.6979 by inning 8. Soccer starts lower and drops further, from 0.8209 bits at kickoff to 0.4394 by minute 90. Soccer therefore ends far more decided, which is consistent with its lower Live-Clock Fraction.

entries.q: Compare model performance at the very start versus the very end of a game.

a.answer: It degrades in both sports. MLB model skill starts at -0.0479 and ends at -0.1926; soccer starts at -0.0599 and ends at -1.1476. The market moves the opposite way in MLB, from 0.013 up to 0.3254 by inning 9. Late-game state is where the model's blind spots cost the most.

entries.q: Which is the bigger problem, miscalibration or missing information?

a.answer: Missing information, by roughly three to one on the MLB in-game moneyline: the reliability gap is +0.0066 while the resolution gap is -0.0235. Recalibration addresses the first and cannot touch the second, so the honest description of the shortfall is a feed problem rather than a fitting problem.

entries.q: Compare how many entity cards each sport has.
alt_phrasings: how many player pages per sport

a.answer: The atlas holds 1,549 cards across seven packs. NBA players is the largest single pack at 482 entries, gated by a floor of at least 800 career minutes, which admits 482 of 807 eligible players. Cards are descriptive summaries, not projections.

entries.q: Which is more informative, the score or the market price?
alt_phrasings: does the price know more than the score

a.answer: The price, consistently. The Market Foresight Premium is positive at every measured checkpoint in both sports -- 0.063 to 0.5208 across MLB innings, 0.6393 to 1.7056 across soccer minutes -- meaning the market resolves more per bit of remaining uncertainty than a scoreboard-only forecaster does. The measurement cannot separate genuine market news from model misspecification.

entries.q: Which sport should I trust these numbers on most?

a.answer: MLB for in-game work and NBA for market structure. MLB carries 78,986 graded in-game rows and 693,037 pitches; NBA is the only sport with a buildable reliability map (1,593 games, 77 buckets, market ECE 0.0064). Soccer and tennis are consistently the thinnest -- soccer at 9,003 in-game rows, tennis with no reliability map at all.

entries.q: Which sport should I trust these numbers on least?

a.answer: Tennis, on coverage grounds: it has no reliability map so the cross-sport structure module records it not_buildable, no blowout corpus so Live-Clock Fraction is not buildable, and its line half-life cannot be pinned inside the 6h+ bucket. Soccer is next, with in-game samples in the hundreds per checkpoint and buckets as small as n=21 in the overreaction work.

entries.q: Is any sport's market beatable?

a.answer: Nothing in the committed evidence supports naming one. Every pregame candidate across six corpora and four sports was rejected under the conjunction gate, and in-game the model's Brier trails the market's at every grain measured -- BSS versus market -0.1502 in MLB and -0.5967 in soccer. Three MLB late-inning distributional rows read provisionally sharper on samples of about twenty, which is not a basis for any claim.

entries.q: How do you decide whether a signal is real?
alt_phrasings: how do you validate a signal

a.answer: A candidate must clear a conjunction, not any one test: BSS>0 AND Diebold-Mariano p<0.05 AND N>=200, replicated on at least two independent corpora, with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR applied across the family. A single-corpus or single-fold lift is treated as an artifact by default, not as evidence.

entries.q: What does leak-free mean here?
alt_phrasings: how do you prevent data leakage

a.answer: States are sorted by timestamp and the model trains only on rows strictly before the evaluation point, in an expanding walk-forward window with purge and embargo between train and test. Any fitted transform -- including slope fits -- happens inside the training window, never on the full sample.

entries.q: Why walk-forward instead of random cross-validation?

a.answer: Because random folds let the future train the past. Sports data is ordered and heavily autocorrelated within a season, so shuffled folds leak information backwards and produce lifts that vanish out of sample. The expanding walk-forward window with purge and embargo reproduces the only situation that matters: predicting a game with information that actually existed beforehand.

entries.q: What does the walk-forward win probability model score?
alt_phrasings: how good is the walk forward model

a.answer: Across 3 folds it averages 0.7094 accuracy (std 0.0252, range 0.6762 to 0.7373) and a mean Brier of 0.19301 (std 0.00841). Each fold is a 5-way non-negative-least-squares blend of XGBoost, LightGBM, logistic regression, an MLP and naive Bayes, and the weights move sharply between folds -- fold 2 leans XGBoost at 0.382, fold 3 leans logistic regression at 0.686.

entries.q: Why do the model weights change so much between folds?

a.answer: Because each fold refits the blend on its own validation slice, and with n_val=491 per fold the meta-learner has limited data to separate similar base models. Fold 2 puts 0.382 on XGBoost and 0.0 on logistic regression; fold 3 flips to 0.686 on logistic regression and 0.108 on XGBoost. The base-model Briers are close enough that the blend is nearly indifferent, which is itself a caution against reading any single fold's weights as a finding.

entries.q: What is devigging and why does it matter?

a.answer: Posted odds include the book's margin, so the implied probabilities sum to more than one. Devigging strips that margin out to recover the market's actual probability estimate. Without it you would be comparing a calibrated forecast against a number that is deliberately biased, and any apparent skill would just be the vig.

entries.q: Which devigging method do you use?
alt_phrasings: how do you remove the vig

a.answer: Shin devigging. The benchmark is stated throughout as the Shin-devigged closing line, and the leak-free forecaster is scored against it on the same real outcomes rather than against raw posted prices.

entries.q: What is the Diebold-Mariano test doing in the gate?
alt_phrasings: how do you test forecast difference

a.answer: It asks whether a loss difference between two forecasts is bigger than sampling noise. The gate forms d_t = loss_close - loss_model and runs a cluster-robust version of the test, so correlated observations inside a game or a day do not inflate significance. SHIP requires DM p<0.05 alongside BSS>0 and N>=200.

entries.q: What is the overfit signature you keep mentioning?

a.answer: A positive full-sample lift that reverses sign on the held-out half. Every pregame candidate that looked promising showed it, and the documented example is an MLB CLV-capture signal worth +0.108pp on the National League slice and -0.017pp on the American League slice -- not replicable across independent corpora, so REJECT.

entries.q: Has anything ever passed the pregame gate?

a.answer: No. Nothing survived the conjunction of two corpora, DM p<0.05 and N>=200 as a market-beating pregame signal, across six corpora and four sports. Every schedule, fatigue, form, head-to-head and totals candidate was rejected, and the NBA home-court probe came in at BSS 0.0000 with DM p=0.173 on N=1,156 because home-court advantage is already fully inside the devig.

entries.q: What is the claim ledger?

a.answer: A per-sport append-only record of every named mechanism the system has tested, with its verdict and an evidence pointer. Across four sports it holds 287 entries: 130 confirmed, 126 null and 31 not-testable. A null or not-testable is recorded as honest market-efficiency evidence, not deleted.

entries.q: How many claims have been confirmed versus rejected?
alt_phrasings: how many nulls do you have

a.answer: Counted across the five ledgers in the honesty exhibit, nulls outnumber confirms 351 to 168, a ratio of 2.1 to 1. The per-sport split is NBA 45 confirmed of 85, MLB 32 of 86, soccer 29 of 64 and tennis 24 of 52; the interaction factory contributes 1,003 entries of which 709 are not-testable.

entries.q: How do you bucket a verdict as confirmed?

a.answer: Confirmed covers exactly four labels: ARTIFACT_CONFIRMED, CONFIRMED_LOCAL, CONFIRMED_LOCAL_incl_2026_OOS and REPLICATED. Not-testable covers NOT_REPLICABLE_NO_CORPUS and NOT_TESTABLE. Everything else -- NULL, NULL_LOCAL, REJECT, PARTIAL, PROVISIONAL, FAILED_REPLICATION -- buckets to null, so the confirmed bucket cannot quietly absorb a weak result.

entries.q: Do claims ever change verdict?

a.answer: Yes, and the history is kept. Across 259 claim families the current statuses are 121 verified, 4 provisional, 99 null, 28 not-testable and 7 retracted, with families that changed status flagged as flipped. Six of the seven retractions are MLB.

entries.q: What is the ratio of nulls to confirmations?

a.answer: 1.107 nulls or worse per confirmation on the claim-family scoreboard: 121 confirms against 134 nulls-or-worse out of 259 families. That ratio is presented as the product, on the reasoning that a system that only ever confirmed would not be credible.

entries.q: What is the reject graveyard?

a.answer: The permanent record of signals that failed. It carries 804 total verdict rows across all reruns, of which 68 distinct sport-signal pairs currently sit on a REJECT-family verdict as of their latest test, and 628 rows are rejects. The gap between 804 and 68 is signals retested multiple times plus rows whose latest verdict flipped to SHIP.

entries.q: What are the most common reasons a signal gets rejected?

a.answer: By recorded reason category the largest is the as-of reclaim sweep at 510 rows -- signals killed when recomputed with strictly as-of information -- followed by prescreen delta 20, walk-forward ablation 18, seed stability 17, calibration-only-unproven 13, discovered transform 10, sealed holdout 8, conformal width 7 and cross-corpus adjudication 6.

entries.q: How many signals have shipped versus been rejected?

a.answer: Across the full 804-row verdict history: 627 REJECT, 95 SHIP, 45 SHIP_REVIEW, 14 NOT_TESTABLE, 6 WORSE, 6 INSUFFICIENT, 4 NOT-REPLICATED, 3 STANDING_BASELINE_SET, and one each of DEFER, TIER3_BLOCKED, UNDERPOWERED and NULL_UNDERPOWERED. A SHIP here means the signal cleared the calibration gate, not that it beats a market price.

entries.q: What is the as-of reclaim sweep?
alt_phrasings: why do signals die on as-of recomputation

a.answer: A re-test of existing signals using only information available at the moment of prediction rather than the season-complete tables they were first computed from. It is the single largest killer in the reject ledger, accounting for 510 of the recorded reject rows -- most apparent signal was subtle hindsight.

entries.q: How big is the claims corpus?
alt_phrasings: how many claims do you have
how many facts in the system

a.answer: 103 claim families holding 103,048 generated claims. 99 of the 103 families carry a validation sidecar, and 101,865 claims were sampled for validation, of which 101,864 verified and 1 was unverifiable -- 0 mismatches.

entries.q: Are all the claims independently verified?

a.answer: 98.85% of generated claims are covered by a validation sample, with 0 recorded mismatches. The honest caveat is stated in the artifact itself: those verified counts are sidecar sample counts, not full-corpus audits, so 'generated' claims outnumber 'verified' claims by design.

entries.q: How are claims distributed across sports?
alt_phrasings: which sport has the most claims

a.answer: NBA dominates with 31 families and 62,227 claims, ahead of MLB (18 families, 21,519), tennis (16 families, 13,709), soccer (15 families, 4,275) and an unlabeled cross-sport group (13 families, 1,236). Claim volume tracks corpus depth, not confidence -- soccer has fewer claims because it has less committed data, not because it is better understood.

entries.q: How do you test the answer layer itself?
alt_phrasings: do you test the ask ai

a.answer: With a regression bank over the resolver: 87 entries, 87 passing, 0 failing, at the FULL tier. It checks fail-closed status and receipt correctness rather than prose quality -- and a correct no_data, not_supported or ambiguous is scored as a PASS, not a failure.

entries.q: How many questions can the system actually answer?
alt_phrasings: what fraction of questions get an answer

a.answer: On a 1,307-row coverage stress test, 863 rows were expected to produce an answer and 316 did -- a coverage rate of 0.3662. The headline deliberately excludes rows where no answer was expected, because a correct no_data or refusal there is a design pass rather than coverage.

entries.q: What statuses can an answer come back with?

a.answer: Five, and each has a mandated behavior: ok returns the value with its receipt; no_data means the artifact is absent or zero-row and the miss must be named; not_supported means the question is outside the registry and must not be improvised; ambiguous means several different mechanisms matched; refused means the question asked for edge, ROI or a retracted number.

entries.q: What does NO_DATA actually mean when you say it?
alt_phrasings: why do you say no data

a.answer: That the artifact behind the question is absent or has zero matching rows, so there is nothing to quote. It is a designed outcome, not an error: the contract requires naming the zero-row miss rather than substituting a plausible number, and the regression bank counts a correct no_data as a pass.

entries.q: How does the system distribute across those statuses in practice?
alt_phrasings: how often does it say no data

a.answer: Over all 1,307 stress rows: 399 ok, 560 no_data, 42 not_supported, 181 ambiguous, 125 refused and 0 errors. More no_data than ok is the expected shape when the corpus is fixed and the question space is not.

entries.q: What happens if I ask a question about stale data?
alt_phrasings: how old can the data be

entries.q: Who wrote this code?

a.answer: Overwhelmingly agents, under one human director. Of 3,224 commits between 2026-03-09 and 2026-07-22, 95.75% are agent-authored and 67.9% carry a Claude co-author trailer. The human decisions were architecture, direction and what may be claimed.

entries.q: How long did this take to build?

a.answer: 3,224 commits over roughly four and a half months, from 2026-03-09 to 2026-07-22, in bursts rather than a steady drip -- the opening day alone carries 64 commits. The daily commit series is published rather than summarized.

entries.q: If agents wrote the code, who is accountable for the claims?

a.answer: The gate is, and it is mechanical. Agents can propose and implement anything, but a claim only becomes publishable by clearing the leak-free gate on two corpora, and the reject ledger's 804 recorded verdict rows against 95 SHIPs shows how often the answer is no. Autonomy in writing code is not autonomy in asserting results.

entries.q: How do you know the published modules still run?

a.answer: Every showcase module is re-executed in a single check run and its status recorded per module with a timestamp and a wall-clock duration -- for example brier_skill_scores.py PASS in 2.94s and aging_curve_lite.py PASS in 1.71s on the 2026-07-24 run. The site manifest carries the aggregate: 63 of 63 checks green.

entries.q: How many analysis modules are there?

a.answer: 54 modules and 1,549 atlas entity cards, all built from the same output directory and all carrying edge_claimed=false. The manifest records 63 of 63 checks green at build time.

entries.q: Why do some modules have a null as_of?

a.answer: Because their underlying computation does not stamp one, and the manifest records null rather than inventing a date. Others carry an as_of that is a corpus description rather than a timestamp -- cf_star_removal reads '2024-25 (Elo end-of-season) x 2024_25 on/off slice' and ctx_lineup_proxy reads '2025-26 regular season (through 2026-04-12)' -- which is more useful than a build time.

entries.q: What is a Brier score?

a.answer: The mean squared error of a probability against a binary outcome: lower is better, and 0.25 is what you get by always saying 50%. It is the primary yardstick here because it punishes both miscalibration and vagueness, unlike accuracy which only asks whether you picked the right side.

entries.q: What is a Brier skill score?
alt_phrasings: what is skill relative to a baseline

a.answer: BSS = 1 - Brier/Brier_ref, the fractional improvement over a reference forecast. Two references are used here: climatology, meaning a constant sport-level base rate, and the market. A BSS above 0 against climatology is easy; against the market it is the only number that would matter, and it is negative everywhere measured.

entries.q: What is ECE?
alt_phrasings: how do you measure calibration error

a.answer: Expected calibration error: bin the forecasts, compare the mean predicted probability to the mean outcome inside each bin, and take the n-weighted mean absolute gap. This system computes it over 10 bins. It isolates calibration specifically -- a forecast can have a decent Brier and still be systematically overconfident.

entries.q: What is the Murphy decomposition and why use it?

a.answer: It splits a Brier score into reliability -- how miscalibrated you are -- and resolution -- how much genuine discrimination you have. That matters diagnostically: on MLB in-game moneyline the model's reliability gap versus the market is +0.0066 while the resolution gap is -0.0235, so the shortfall is mostly missing information, which recalibration cannot fix.

entries.q: Why does it matter whether a gap is reliability or resolution?

a.answer: Because only one of them is cheap to fix. A reliability gap means the probabilities are systematically off and a recalibration map can close it; a resolution gap means the model does not know things the market knows, and no post-processing invents information. The MLB decomposition puts most of the gap in resolution, which is an honest statement about missing feeds rather than about the fitting procedure.

entries.q: What floors do you apply before publishing a number?
alt_phrasings: when do you refuse to report

a.answer: They are per-module and always declared. The Brier skill module requires n>=30 rows per grain; calibration by market type requires n>=30 usable rows for a Brier or ECE over 10 bins; the count-leverage module uses a class minimum of 500 pitches; Line Half-Life requires at least 20 move pairs. Below the floor the cell is flagged rather than filled.

entries.q: What do you do when a corpus has no resolved outcomes?

a.answer: Disclose it rather than score it. The MLB in-game totals quote-tracks -- 5 files, 2,113 rows, 21 quote-tracks -- carry no resolved outcome because the settlement join is unavailable, so their Brier is null by design and only the model-versus-market divergence is reported (median 0.116128, mean 0.124782, p90 0.224736). Scoring them would require fabricating labels.

entries.q: How do you avoid double-counting duplicate corpora?

a.answer: By identifying byte-identical duplicates and excluding them explicitly. The mlb_clean moneyline corpus is a byte-identical duplicate of mlb and is skipped with the reason recorded in the artifact, so the 78,986-row MLB moneyline sample is not silently counted twice.

entries.q: What is the point of the honesty exhibit?

a.answer: To make the null rate a headline instead of a footnote. Its own summary line is that nulls (351) outnumber confirms (168) by 2.1x, published per sport with the source ledger path for each. A research surface that reports only its wins gives you no way to price its claims.

entries.q: Why do you compare against the market instead of just reporting accuracy?
alt_phrasings: why is the market the benchmark

a.answer: Because accuracy has no scale. A 71% accurate NBA win-probability model sounds strong until you notice the closing line does at least as well on the same games. The devigged close is a live, adversarial, well-capitalized benchmark, so scoring against it is the only test that can distinguish a good model from an easy sample.

entries.q: What is the difference between a confirmed mechanism and a shipped signal?

a.answer: Different bars entirely. A confirmed mechanism, like b2b_rest_penalty at -1.73 pts/100 ORtg (n=4,732, p=0.0056), is a described effect in one corpus, labeled CONFIRMED_LOCAL. A shipped signal has to clear the leak-free gate on two corpora against the devigged close. 130 mechanisms are confirmed; nothing has shipped as a market-beating pregame signal.

entries.q: What does CONFIRMED_LOCAL mean?

a.answer: The effect held in the specific corpus it was tested on, and nowhere else has been checked. The back-to-back rest penalty carries it twice at different sample cuts -- -1.73 pts/100 at n=4,732, p=0.0056 and -1.955 at n=7,192, p=0.000117 -- both on the same 2024-25/2025-26 boxscore corpus. Anything derived from a CONFIRMED_LOCAL effect inherits its single-corpus limit.

entries.q: How many mechanisms have been tested per sport?

a.answer: NBA leads at 85 tested mechanisms (45 confirmed, 33 null, 7 not-testable), with MLB at 86, soccer at 64 and tennis at 52 in the honesty exhibit's count. The four ledgers total 287 rows in the mechanism export.

entries.q: Why are so many claims not-testable?

a.answer: Almost all of them come from one place: the interaction factory, which generated 1,003 candidate claims of which 709 are not-testable. Machine-generated interaction hypotheses routinely reference slices with no corpus behind them, and marking them not-testable is more honest than testing them on a proxy and reporting the proxy's answer.

entries.q: How many claims failed replication?

a.answer: Failed replications are counted per ledger: 7 in MLB, 1 in soccer and 17 in the interaction factory, with none recorded in NBA or tennis. A failed replication is kept as its own category rather than folded back into the null bucket.

entries.q: What is the difference between the in-game and pregame validation?
alt_phrasings: how do you validate live models

a.answer: Pregame is scored against the Shin-devigged closing line on completed games under the leak-free gate. In-game is scored tick by tick against the live market at recorded checkpoints, using Brier skill against both the market and a constant base rate -- 78,986 MLB rows and 9,003 soccer rows in the current pack. Neither uses a live feed; both read committed, settled corpora.

entries.q: What is the forecaster proof pack?

a.answer: Six committed aggregates assembled behind the forecaster page: walk-forward win-probability results, state-conditioned calibration, the Murphy decomposition, calibration stability, Brier skill scores and the cross-sport scoreboard. The manifest also names what it could not include -- two uncommitted in-game grade-join caches -- rather than quietly citing them.

a.answer: The forecaster manifest documents one such case explicitly: the in-game proof document cites source scripts and a raw settlement-join cache rather than a committed JSON receipt for its headline figure, so the pack substitutes already-verified committed aggregates over the same corpus. Naming the gap is the practice; papering over it is not.

entries.q: What is the truth source for a number on this site?

a.answer: The evidence packet governs what may be claimed, and every module points back to it. Modules that touch marketable ground -- calibration by market type, the Brier skill pack -- name it as truth_source in the artifact itself, and the answer contract requires quoting source_artifact and as_of with any number.

entries.q: Why does every module say edge_claimed false?

a.answer: It is a machine-checkable stamp that the module is a calibration or description artifact, not a profit claim. It appears on the showcase manifest, on every novel-stat card and on the Brier skill pack, and it is the reason a question phrased in ROI or bankroll terms comes back refused rather than answered.

entries.q: What is the cross-sport structure check for?

a.answer: Running one reliability-map methodology across sports so their numbers are comparable, and refusing to produce a number where the floors are not met. It requires n_games>=30 per bucket with a non-null market mean probability; NBA passes with 1,593 games and 77 usable buckets, while MLB, soccer and tennis all come back not_buildable with the reason stated.

entries.q: What does 'not buildable' mean?

a.answer: The inputs for that slice do not exist or do not clear the declared floor, so no number is produced at all. In the cross-sport structure module MLB and soccer are not_buildable because no bucket had both a market mean probability and n_games>=30, and tennis because its reliability map file is simply absent. Each reason is written into the artifact.

entries.q: How do you handle overlapping categories in an analysis?

a.answer: By labeling them and refusing to sum them. The MLB count-leverage module marks behind/even/ahead as a mutually exclusive, exhaustive partition while two_strike and three_ball are overlapping lenses whose counts are explicitly not additive with it; the schedule module makes the same declaration about back-to-backs, 3-in-4s and 4-in-6s.

entries.q: How do you report rates so they are not misleading?

a.answer: Every rate is taken over its own non-null denominator rather than the raw class count, which is stated as a floor note in the artifacts that publish rates. In the count-leverage module that means strike and ball rates use n_type and in-zone rates use n_zone, which differ -- 183,042 versus 181,462 in the pitcher-behind class alone.

entries.q: Is any of this a live system?

a.answer: No. Every answer here reads committed artifacts on disk -- settled games, historical odds snapshots, finished seasons -- and there is no live odds or live game-state feed behind the site. Questions about tonight's line, a current score or a live win probability come back as no_data by design rather than being estimated.

entries.q: What would it take to change the headline result?

a.answer: The same conjunction that has rejected everything so far: BSS>0 against the devigged close, Diebold-Mariano p<0.05, N>=200, replicated on at least two independent corpora and surviving Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Until a candidate clears all five simultaneously, the recorded verdict stays 'the market is efficient on every pregame slice measured'.

entries.q: Do you publish the code that runs the gate?

a.answer: Yes -- the proof document names the modules directly, including the Diebold-Mariano implementation under the eval-gate package and the beat-the-close scoreboard entry point, and notes that when the real corpora are absent the harness prints VALIDATION_PENDING and falls back to recorded tables rather than silently reproducing them.

entries.q: What happens if the underlying data is missing when a page builds?

a.answer: The harness declares it. A re-run without the real local corpora prints VALIDATION_PENDING and falls back to the recorded tables rather than emitting a fresh-looking number, and modules whose inputs are absent record not_buildable with the reason. The failure mode is a visible gap, not a plausible fabrication.

a.answer: Through dedicated modules that re-score the same forecaster across time slices -- calibration_over_time and calibration_stability, both included in the forecaster proof pack, with calibration_stability last stamped 2026-07-23. Stability is treated as a separate question from average calibration, because a model can be well-calibrated on average and badly calibrated in every individual period.

entries.q: What are the novel stats?
alt_phrasings: what new metrics did you invent
what original stats do you have

a.answer: Six, each composed only from committed module output and each gated against prior art before publication: Line Half-Life (LHL), Live-Clock Fraction (LCF), Load-Bearing Index (LBI), Market Foresight Premium (MFP), Overreaction Harvest Gap (OHG) and Schedule Fatigue Tax (SFT). All six carry edge_claimed=false. One, OHG, is flagged is_honest_null -- it measures a failure, not a finding.

entries.q: What does the prior-art verdict on each novel stat mean?
alt_phrasings: how do you know nobody invented this already

a.answer: Each stat is labeled by how much of it is genuinely fresh, and the label is deliberately conservative: LHL is NOVEL_PACKAGING, LCF is INCREMENTAL_NOVEL, LBI / MFP / SFT are INCREMENTAL, and OHG is NOVEL_SELF_CRITICAL_CROSS. Every card names the existing literature it sits on top of and instructs the reader not to claim first-ever on the components.

entries.q: Do any of the novel stats claim a betting edge?
alt_phrasings: can I bet these novel stats

a.answer: No, and none of them is built to. All six cards are stamped edge_claimed=false and descriptive_only=true, and the one that comes closest to a market angle -- the Overreaction Harvest Gap -- exists precisely to record that the model cannot cash the overshoot it measures. There is no dollar, ROI or profit figure attached to any of these stats.

entries.q: Which novel stat is an honest null?
alt_phrasings: did any of the novel stats fail

a.answer: The Overreaction Harvest Gap, flagged is_honest_null=true in the index. It measures real market overshoot at large in-game moves and then measures how badly the model fails to convert it: at maximum disagreement the model is closer than the market only 21.52% of the time in soccer_intl and 37.73% in MLB. Publishing that is the point.

entries.q: What is Line Half-Life?
alt_phrasings: what does line half life measure

a.answer: Per sport, the number of hours before tip by which half of the pre-game absolute line motion is complete. It answers a plain question -- when does a sport's price actually get made -- with a single constant per sport instead of a hand-wave about early sharp money.

entries.q: How is Line Half-Life calculated?
alt_phrasings: how do you compute line half life

a.answer: bucket_move = n * mean_abs_move per horizon bucket; G(h) = cumulative far-to-near movement divided by total; the half-life is the h where G(h) = 0.50, linearly interpolated. The inputs come from the micro_absorption module, not from a separate fit.

entries.q: Which sport's betting line settles earliest?
alt_phrasings: which sport moves its line first

a.answer: Of the five sports measured, soccer_intl settles fastest: half its pre-game line motion is done 2.75 hours before kickoff (half_life_hours 2.7461, n_move_pairs 164,072). MLB follows at 3.67h and NBA at 4.76h.

entries.q: What is the NBA's line half-life?
alt_phrasings: when does the nba line settle

a.answer: 4.76 hours (half_life_hours 4.7567) over 182,054 pre-game move pairs -- the slowest of the three sports whose crossing can be pinned. NBA is also the most back-loaded: 32.47% of its total absolute motion lands in the final hour before tip, so the single constant hides a bimodal shape.

entries.q: What is MLB's line half-life?
alt_phrasings: when does the mlb line settle

a.answer: 3.67 hours (half_life_hours 3.6709), measured over 1,307,128 pre-game move pairs -- by far the largest sample of the five. Only 18.13% of MLB's absolute motion arrives in the final hour, the steadiest profile in the set.

entries.q: Which sports have no measurable line half-life?
alt_phrasings: which sports move their line more than 6 hours out

a.answer: Tennis and WNBA both cross the 50% mark inside the open-ended 6h+ bucket, so their half-life is reported as '>6.0' with half_life_hours=null rather than guessed. By 6 hours out tennis has already completed 54.26% of its motion and WNBA 64.41%.

entries.q: Why is soccer excluded from Line Half-Life?
alt_phrasings: why no soccer line half life
which sports were dropped from lhl

a.answer: Domestic soccer is excluded as a timestamp-coverage artifact: all its mass sits in the 6h+ bucket with mean_abs_move 0.0, which is a data defect rather than a finding. KBO and NPB are excluded too, both with 0 pre-game move pairs against a MIN_MOVES floor of 20. soccer_intl, a separate corpus, does qualify.

entries.q: Is Line Half-Life actually a new idea?
alt_phrasings: has line half life been done before

a.answer: Only the packaging. The card is labeled NOVEL_PACKAGING and cites the existing work directly: opening-versus-closing line timing is discussed everywhere in the betting press, and price-impact half-life is a securities-microstructure staple (Kyle 1985; Amihud 2002). What is fresh is the single per-sport half-life constant, not the underlying concept.

entries.q: What are the weaknesses of Line Half-Life?
alt_phrasings: what's wrong with line half life

a.answer: Five are declared on the card. bucket_move sums absolute per-tick moves, so it is churn rather than net price travel and correlated books inflate it; there are only four coarse horizon buckets so the 0.50 crossing is interpolated; soccer is a coverage artifact; NBA is bimodal and a single half-life hides that; and any sport crossing inside the open 6h+ bucket cannot be pinned at all.

entries.q: How much line movement happens in the final hour before a game?
alt_phrasings: how much moves right before tip

a.answer: It varies more than three-fold across sports: NBA 32.47%, soccer_intl 26.10%, MLB 18.13%, WNBA 11.76%, tennis 10.70%. NBA being the most back-loaded is the reason its single half-life reads misleadingly slow.

entries.q: What is the Live-Clock Fraction?
alt_phrasings: what does live clock fraction measure

a.answer: The 0-to-1 share of a sport's game clock that stays genuinely contested before the score gap crosses a point of no return, taken at a near-median margin threshold. Higher means the sport stays live later.

entries.q: Which sport stays competitive the longest?
alt_phrasings: mlb vs soccer live clock fraction

a.answer: Of the two sports that could be built, MLB stays contested later: LCF 0.8333 versus soccer_intl 0.7475. The ranking is indicative rather than metric -- a 3-run threshold in baseball and a 1-goal threshold in soccer are not equated quantities, and innings and minutes are different clock units.

entries.q: Why is there no NBA Live-Clock Fraction?
alt_phrasings: why no basketball live clock fraction
