a.answer: NBA and tennis have no blowout corpus, so LCF is not buildable for them and the card records that as an explicit not_buildable rather than filling a number. NBA does get an independent decisiveness cross-check from a different module: a comeback rate of 0.0146 and a favorite hold rate of 0.9854.

entries.q: How often do NBA favorites blow a near-decided game?
alt_phrasings: how often does the nba favorite hold

a.answer: Once the in-game market price crosses 0.85, the favorite holds 98.54% of the time and the comeback rate is 1.46%, measured over 23 usable buckets, 171,220 ticks and 5,578 games. This is a market-price-conditioned rate, not a score-margin rule.

entries.q: How is the Live-Clock Fraction threshold chosen?
alt_phrasings: how do you pick the lcf margin threshold

a.answer: LCF is the decided_clockfrac_median at the non-masked threshold whose decided_frac_of_games is closest to 0.50. In MLB that lands on a 3-run threshold (decided_frac 0.5337, 95 of 178 games); soccer_intl has only one non-masked threshold, 1 goal (decided_frac 0.4828, 14 of 29 games), so no choice is actually exercised there.

entries.q: Is the Live-Clock Fraction a new method?
alt_phrasings: has live clock fraction been done

a.answer: Partly, and the card says so: it is labeled INCREMENTAL_NOVEL, citing Bill James safe-lead heuristics and win-probability clinch points as existing within-sport method. Only the normalized cross-sport live-clock axis is claimed as the contribution.

entries.q: How small are the Live-Clock Fraction samples?
alt_phrasings: how many games in the lcf measurement

a.answer: Small enough to read carefully: MLB is 178 total games with 95 decided at the near-median threshold, and soccer_intl is 29 total games with 14 decided. The cross-sport ranking should be treated as indicative on those counts.

entries.q: What is the Load-Bearing Index?
alt_phrasings: what does load bearing index measure

a.answer: Per NBA team, how much of its win probability rides on its single most indispensable player, estimated two independent ways and flagged for whether the two agree. Estimator (a) is the max player-level Elo on/off win-prob delta; estimator (b) is the max raw win-rate gap between games a player was active and games he missed.

entries.q: Which NBA team is most dependent on one player?
alt_phrasings: which team is most fragile without its star

a.answer: Denver, on the Elo on/off estimator: Nikola Jokic carries a delta_winprob of 0.5822 with an on/off net-rating delta of 23.713 -- the largest single-player figure among the 30 teams. Read it as a dependence description, not a causal player-impact estimate.

entries.q: What is Oklahoma City's Load-Bearing Index?
alt_phrasings: how dependent is okc on sga

a.answer: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander leads the Elo on/off estimator at delta_winprob 0.5171 with an on/off net-rating delta of 15.763, second-highest among the 30 teams. The raw with/without estimator names a different player for OKC (Ajay Mitchell, delta_win_rate 0.2685 over 57 active and 23 missed games), which is the norm rather than the exception here.

entries.q: Do the two Load-Bearing Index estimators agree?
alt_phrasings: do both methods name the same player
how consistent is the load bearing index

a.answer: Almost never. Across the 30 teams covered by both estimators, only 1 agrees on the same #1 player -- an agree_rate of 0.0333. That team is Indiana, where both name Pascal Siakam (Elo delta_winprob 0.3872; raw delta_win_rate 0.2075 over 62 active and 15 missed games).

entries.q: Why do the Load-Bearing Index estimators disagree so much?
alt_phrasings: is the load bearing index unreliable

a.answer: Mostly because they are not measuring the same season or the same quantity. Estimator (a) uses 2024-25 Elo end-of-season on/off, estimator (b) uses the 2025-26 regular season through 2026-04-12, so agreement is directional corroboration and not a paired estimate. On top of that, (a) is win probability against a league-average opponent on a neutral floor while (b) is raw team win rate active-versus-missed -- related axes, different scales.

entries.q: Is the Load-Bearing Index a causal measure of player impact?
alt_phrasings: does lbi prove a player's value

a.answer: No, and the card labels this the first declared confound. Both estimators inherit the roster confound their source files flag: why a player missed is entangled with injury clustering, rest, blowout pulls and replacement lineup quality, none of which is controlled. It is a fragility description, not a causal player-impact estimate.

entries.q: Is the Load-Bearing Index original?
alt_phrasings: has on off fragility been published

a.answer: Incremental, per its own label. The card cites inpredictable's On/Off Win Probability tables, standard record-without-star splits and arXiv 1604.03186 on player impact on win chances, and states plainly that single-method fragility is not new. The claimed twist is a league-wide fragility ranking cross-validated by two independent estimators with an agreement flag.

entries.q: Which teams show the biggest raw with-without swing?
alt_phrasings: largest with without win rate gap
biggest raw win rate gap nba

a.answer: On the raw estimator the largest gaps come with small missed-game samples, which is the warning label. Milwaukee's Kyle Kuzma shows delta_win_rate 0.3659 on 69 active and 12 missed games, and the Clippers' Brook Lopez 0.4038 on 75 active and just 7 missed. Seven-game denominators do not support a strong reading.

entries.q: What is the Lakers' load-bearing player?

a.answer: The two estimators disagree, and the Elo one names a role player rather than a star: Dorian Finney-Smith at delta_winprob 0.4656 with an on/off net-rating delta of 14.944, while the raw with/without estimator names Rui Hachimura at delta_win_rate 0.2626 over 68 active and 14 missed games. Neither is a causal claim about who matters most.

entries.q: What is the Market Foresight Premium?
alt_phrasings: what does market foresight premium measure

a.answer: The market's excess resolving power over a scoreboard-only model, per bit of uncertainty still left in the game, measured checkpoint by checkpoint. It is a way of asking how much the market knows that the score alone does not, normalized so late-game checkpoints do not automatically dominate.

entries.q: How is the Market Foresight Premium computed?

a.answer: MFP(t) = ((naive - market)/naive - (naive - model)/naive) / max(entropy_market_bits, 0.15). The 0.15-bit entropy floor exists because entropy heading to zero late in a game would otherwise explode the ratio.

entries.q: How does the Market Foresight Premium behave in MLB?
alt_phrasings: does the market's edge grow during a game

a.answer: It rises steadily through the game: 0.063 at the first inning checkpoint (n=7,646), 0.2513 by inning 6, 0.4182 at inning 7 and peaking at 0.5208 at inning 9 (n=2,282), with a mean of 0.2461 across 10 checkpoints. The last checkpoint drops back to 0.2365 on only 94 rows.

entries.q: How does the Market Foresight Premium behave in soccer?

a.answer: Much higher throughout and still rising: 0.6393 at kickoff, 0.7877 by minute 30, and 1.7056 at the minute-90 checkpoint, with a mean of 0.9211 over 19 checkpoints and a first-to-last delta of 1.0663. Soccer checkpoint samples are thin -- the 90-minute row is n=37.

entries.q: In which sport does the market have the biggest in-game information advantage?
alt_phrasings: where is the market sharpest in game
which sport has the highest market foresight premium

a.answer: Soccer, by a wide margin: mean MFP 0.9211 versus 0.2461 in MLB, and a final-checkpoint value of 1.7056 versus 0.2365. The two are not strictly equated -- MLB is measured per inning and soccer per 5-minute bucket -- so read the gap as large but not a precise multiple.

entries.q: Does a high Market Foresight Premium mean our model is bad?
alt_phrasings: is mfp measuring market news or model error
what does a high mfp really mean

a.answer: It cannot separate the two, and the card says so. The 'model' side is one specific state-only forecaster, so MFP conflates genuine news the market prices -- lineups, momentum, injuries -- with plain model misspecification. The honest reading is that the market resolves more per bit than a scoreboard-only view, not that any particular cause has been isolated.

entries.q: What prior work does the Market Foresight Premium build on?

a.answer: Two established literatures. The absorption instrument -- paired model/market/naive Brier by game-time -- is arXiv 2606.07811 on when markets fully process public information, which the source module already flags INCREMENTAL, and entropy decay is textbook Shannon. Only the skill-gap-per-bit normalization crossing the two is claimed.

entries.q: What is the model's in-game skill score at each MLB checkpoint?
alt_phrasings: is the model negative skill in game

a.answer: Negative at every one of the 10 MLB checkpoints in this module, ranging from -0.0184 at inning 5 to -0.1926 at the final checkpoint, while market skill runs from 0.013 up to 0.3254. Against a naive baseline the market resolves the game and this state-only model does not.

entries.q: What is the Overreaction Harvest Gap?
alt_phrasings: what does overreaction harvest gap measure

a.answer: Structural market overshoot at large in-game moves, scaled by how far short the model falls of beating the market when the two disagree most. It is deliberately a measured failure diagnostic: the market moves too far, and we still cannot exploit it.

entries.q: What is the Overreaction Harvest Gap in soccer?

a.answer: soccer_intl shows an overreaction magnitude of 0.2856 but a model_closer_rate of only 0.2152 at maximum disagreement (n=4,406), giving an OHG of 0.0813. Read literally: the market overshoots and is still right about four times in five when we disagree hardest with it.

entries.q: What is the Overreaction Harvest Gap in MLB?

a.answer: MLB overshoots much less -- overreaction magnitude 0.0721 -- and the model_closer_rate at maximum disagreement is 0.3773 over 33,402 rows, giving an OHG of 0.0088. Smaller overshoot, still no harvest.

entries.q: When the model and the market disagree most, who is right?
alt_phrasings: model closer rate at high disagreement
is the model right when it disagrees

a.answer: The market, in both sports measured. At the >=.10 disagreement bucket the model's Brier is 0.282705 against the market's 0.210258 in MLB (n=33,402), and 0.330582 against 0.172027 in soccer_intl (n=4,406). Both rows carry market_usually_right_at_max_disagree=true.

entries.q: Doesn't market overreaction mean there's money on the table?

a.answer: Not on this evidence, and that is exactly why the stat exists. The card's first declared confound is mandatory language: OHG is an honest null, and at maximum disagreement the market is usually right (model_closer_rate 0.38 in MLB, 0.22 in soccer). Overshoot that we cannot identify in advance is not a tradable quantity, and no dollar figure is attached anywhere.

entries.q: How large are the overreaction buckets?
alt_phrasings: how noisy is the overreaction measurement

a.answer: MLB is reasonably sized -- 2,860 rows in the 3-6pt bucket, 1,069 in 6-10pt, 794 in 10pt+ -- with overshoot falling from 0.0801 to 0.0518 as moves get bigger. Soccer is thin: 103, 21 and 91 rows respectively, so its 0.2856 magnitude is explicitly flagged noisy.

entries.q: What prior work does the Overreaction Harvest Gap build on?

a.answer: Overreaction and reversion are Moskowitz (2021, Journal of Finance) and Choi & Hui (2014, JEBO), and disagreement skill is standard forecast verification -- the card flags both components as not new. Its verdict, NOVEL_SELF_CRITICAL_CROSS, claims only the crossing: 'the market is wrong and we still cannot cash it' is a confession, and papers publish edges rather than confessions.

entries.q: What is the Schedule Fatigue Tax?
alt_phrasings: what does schedule fatigue tax measure

a.answer: Per team-season, the points tax from back-to-back congestion: the team's back-to-back frequency multiplied by the tested back-to-back performance penalty. It converts a schedule quirk into a season-averaged points figure so teams can be compared on the same axis.

entries.q: How is the Schedule Fatigue Tax calculated?

a.answer: SFT_credible = b2b_freq * (-1.73 pts/100 ORtg), with a descriptive companion SFT_descriptive = b2b_freq * (-0.315 composite per 36). The -1.73 anchor is not invented here; it is copied from the repo's own tested b2b_rest_penalty mechanism receipt.

entries.q: Which NBA team has the most punishing schedule?
alt_phrasings: worst back to back schedule nba

a.answer: Denver in 2025-26: 17 back-to-backs, a b2b_freq of 0.218, and a season-averaged SFT of -0.3771 pts/100 ORtg -- the largest of 90 team-seasons. Atlanta and Houston in 2024-25 follow at -0.3633 each.

entries.q: Which NBA team has the easiest schedule by fatigue?

a.answer: Memphis in 2025-26: 12 back-to-backs, b2b_freq 0.156, SFT -0.2699 pts/100 ORtg -- the smallest tax in the 90 team-seasons measured. Atlanta and Chicago in 2025-26 sit just above it at -0.2733.

entries.q: How unequal are NBA schedules?
alt_phrasings: how much do back to back counts vary

a.answer: Less than the discourse suggests. Across 90 team-seasons the credible tax spans only 0.1072 pts/100 ORtg end to end (-0.3771 to -0.2699), with a standard deviation of 0.0252. Back-to-back frequency itself ranges from 0.156 to 0.218.

entries.q: Have back-to-backs gotten more common?
alt_phrasings: is the nba schedule getting harder

a.answer: The within-season spread in back-to-back frequency has widened across the three seasons in the corpus: 0.048 in 2023-24, 0.051 in 2024-25, 0.062 in 2025-26. That is a dispersion figure -- teams differing more from each other -- not a league-wide level increase.

entries.q: What evidence backs the back-to-back penalty?

a.answer: A recorded mechanism verdict of CONFIRMED_LOCAL on the claim b2b_rest_penalty: -1.73 pts/100 team ORtg (rested minus back-to-back), n=4,732, p=0.0056. It is a single-corpus local confirmation, which is why the derived tax is labeled descriptive rather than predictive.

entries.q: Is the Schedule Fatigue Tax a new discovery?
alt_phrasings: is back to back fatigue new

a.answer: No, and the card is emphatic about it. The back-to-back fatigue effect is heavily documented -- scoring drops, win-rate drops, standard spread adjustments, and academic work on schedule congestion (ResearchGate 339933590) -- and the instruction is to cite that as prior art. Only the per-team-season aggregation into a points tax plus a league inequality spread is fresh packaging.

entries.q: Can I add up back-to-backs, 3-in-4s and 4-in-6s to get total schedule fatigue?
alt_phrasings: why only b2b in the tax

a.answer: No. The three density classes overlap and are explicitly non-additive, which is why the formula deliberately uses back-to-backs alone -- summing them would double-count the same congested stretches. The card lists this as a declared confound rather than leaving it to the reader.

entries.q: Can I use the Schedule Fatigue Tax to predict games?

a.answer: No. SFT is marked descriptive_only with edge_claimed=false, and its own confound list calls the -1.73 anchor a single-corpus CONFIRMED_LOCAL effect that is 'a descriptive tax, not a forecast, and not re-tested here'. It describes seasons already played; nothing about it has been gated as a forward-looking signal.

entries.q: What are the per-36 numbers behind the Schedule Fatigue Tax?

a.answer: The descriptive companion uses a -0.315 composite-per-36 delta versus rested games, giving team-season values such as -0.0687 for Denver 2025-26 and -0.0491 for Memphis 2025-26. Those per-36 deltas are raw pooled means, not adjusted for roster, opponent, minutes or home-away.

entries.q: How many team-seasons are in the Schedule Fatigue Tax?
alt_phrasings: how many teams in schedule fatigue tax

a.answer: 90 team-seasons, covering 30 teams across three seasons. Every one gets both a credible pts/100 ORtg tax and a descriptive per-36 companion.

entries.q: How were the novel stats built -- are they new models?
alt_phrasings: how are the novel stats computed
did you train a model for the novel stats

a.answer: None of them is a model. The index states the method plainly: composition only, each card copied from its own module's novel_*.json output, which in turn reads existing committed showcase artifacts. Nothing is refit, and every card names the source artifacts it composed.

entries.q: Which novel stat covers the most entities?
alt_phrasings: which novel stat has the most rows

a.answer: Schedule Fatigue Tax, with 90 team-season rows, followed by Load-Bearing Index at 30 teams. The market-structure stats are the thinnest by row count -- Line Half-Life covers 5 sports, and LCF, MFP and OHG cover 2 each -- because they are per-sport rather than per-entity.

entries.q: Which novel stats are about the market rather than the teams?

a.answer: Three of six: Line Half-Life (when the pre-game price gets made), Market Foresight Premium (how much the in-game market knows per bit of remaining uncertainty) and Overreaction Harvest Gap (overshoot we cannot harvest). Load-Bearing Index and Schedule Fatigue Tax are team-side; Live-Clock Fraction is game-structure only and reads the score path, not any price.

entries.q: Do the novel stats agree with each other about which sports are hardest to read?

a.answer: Partly, and the disagreements are informative. Soccer_intl prices earliest (LHL 2.75h), carries the largest in-game market advantage (MFP mean 0.9211) and the largest unharvestable overshoot (OHG 0.0813), while MLB is slower to price (3.67h), has a much smaller market premium (MFP mean 0.2461) and stays contested later (LCF 0.8333). These are separate corpora and different units, so treat the pattern as directional.

entries.q: Which novel stat is the weakest?
alt_phrasings: which new metric should I trust least

a.answer: Live-Clock Fraction, on coverage grounds: it is buildable for only two sports, rests on 178 MLB and 29 soccer_intl games, and its thresholds are not equated across sports, so the ranking is indicative rather than metric. Load-Bearing Index is a close second, since its two estimators agree on only 1 of 30 teams and cover different seasons.

entries.q: Is there a novel stat for tennis?
alt_phrasings: do the new metrics cover tennis

a.answer: Only partially. Tennis appears in Line Half-Life -- where its crossing falls inside the open 6h+ bucket, so it is reported as '>6.0' with a null half-life over 809,986 move pairs -- and is recorded as not_buildable for Live-Clock Fraction because there is no tennis blowout corpus. The other four novel stats do not cover tennis at all.

entries.q: What would make you retract a novel stat?
alt_phrasings: how do you retire a novel stat
would you pull a new metric

a.answer: Two things it is already designed to catch. Each card carries an explicit prior-art citation, so a credible earlier publication of the same construction downgrades or removes it; and each carries declared confounds, so a confound turning out to be the whole effect kills it. Line Half-Life already excludes three sports on data-quality grounds rather than reporting them.

entries.q: Where can I see the novel stats on the site?
alt_phrasings: where are the new metrics published
show me the novel stat cards

a.answer: Each novel stat is composed from modules you can open directly in the browse surface: micro_absorption behind Line Half-Life, blowout_dynamics and xsport_structure behind Live-Clock Fraction, cf_star_removal and ctx_lineup_proxy behind Load-Bearing Index, info_arrival_curve and market_convergence behind Market Foresight Premium, market_overreaction and market_disagreement_profile behind the Overreaction Harvest Gap, and schedule_density behind the Schedule Fatigue Tax.

entries.q: What kind of player is Nikola Jokic, statistically?
alt_phrasings: How good is Jokic by the numbers?

a.answer: Over a 3-season sample Jokic averages 28.4 points, 12.8 rebounds, and 10.1 assists per 36 minutes across 210 games -- a triple-double rate line from the center spot. His shooting is efficient too, at 57.6 percent from the field and 38.9 percent from three. These are per-36 rates over three seasons, not per-game and not opponent-adjusted, and a per-36 triple-double rate is not the same as per-game averages.

entries.q: Is Jokic really passing like a guard from the center position?
alt_phrasings: How good a passer is Jokic for a big?
Does Jokic play like a point-center?

a.answer: His 10.1 assists per 36 minutes is a guard-level playmaking rate from a center, which is the headline of his profile. He pairs that with 12.8 rebounds and 28.4 points per 36 over the 3-season window. It is a raw box rate with no adjustment for teammates or role, so read it as production, not a measured impact number.

entries.q: How efficient is Giannis, and where does he struggle?

a.answer: Giannis posts 32.0 points and 12.1 rebounds per 36 minutes on 60.9 percent shooting -- elite efficiency that mostly reflects a rim-heavy shot diet. The clear weak spots are outside and at the line: 27.4 percent from three and 64.0 percent on free throws. The high field-goal rate is about where the shots come from, not touch from range.

entries.q: Who is the most consistent star game to game?
alt_phrasings: Which player is the steadiest night to night?
Who has the lowest game-to-game variance?

a.answer: Of 579 qualified players, Luka Doncic is the most consistent game to game, with a shrunk composite coefficient of variation of 0.3448 -- well under the league median of 0.6235 -- edging Nikola Jokic at 0.3456. That means their per-36 points, rebounds, and assists barely wobble, roughly half the swing of a median rotation player. Low volatility is not the same as high value, and the measure is descriptive with no opponent or rest adjustment.

entries.q: What does Luka Doncic's production look like?
alt_phrasings: How much does Luka do on the floor?

a.answer: Luka produces 31.9 points, 8.6 assists, and 8.4 rebounds per 36 minutes -- a heavy scoring-plus-playmaking load, with the rebounding rate high for a lead guard. Efficiency is solid but not elite at 47.4 percent from the field and 37.3 percent from three. The numbers are per-36 rates over three seasons and say nothing about usage or shot quality.

entries.q: How efficient is Shai Gilgeous-Alexander for a guard?

a.answer: SGA scores 33.3 points per 36 minutes on unusually clean guard efficiency -- 53.5 percent from the field and 88.4 percent from the line -- across 218 games, among the highest game counts in this pack. High field-goal percentage for a guard often reflects a mid-range and rim-heavy diet, which the raw rate does not separate. It is a per-36 rate over three seasons, not opponent-adjusted.

entries.q: What makes Stephen Curry's profile unusual?
alt_phrasings: How good a shooter is Curry?

a.answer: The shooting is the whole story: 40.0 percent from three and 92.7 percent at the free-throw line, alongside 28.9 points per 36 minutes over 187 games. His overall field-goal mark is a comparatively modest 45.3 percent, which is consistent with a high three-point diet rather than worse touch. Field-goal percentage here is unadjusted for shot location.

entries.q: How efficient is Kevin Durant across the three shooting zones?

a.answer: Durant's line reads 52.3 / 41.8 / 85.8 from the field, three, and the line -- rare efficiency across all three zones -- while scoring 26.0 points per 36 minutes over 215 games. Playmaking is secondary at 4.6 assists per 36, in line with a score-first role. A rate says nothing about usage or the quality of the shots taken.

entries.q: What stands out about Victor Wembanyama's numbers?
alt_phrasings: How good is Victor Wembanyama already?

a.answer: Wembanyama grabs 13.1 rebounds and scores 27.8 points per 36 minutes while stretching to the three-point line at 34.2 percent -- the 13.1 rebounding rate is the highest among the stars profiled in this pack. The sample is still young at 179 games across three seasons. The rebounding comparison is only against these 20 star players, not the full league.

entries.q: Is Wembanyama actually getting better, or is that just hype?
alt_phrasings: Who is the league's biggest form riser?

a.answer: By the box-composite form measure, Wembanyama is the league's biggest riser: his 10-game rolling per-36 box composite climbed +19.821, roughly doubling from 18.048 to 37.869 -- the 100th league percentile. The mirror image is Myles Turner, the biggest faller at -11.043. This is a trajectory read over the whole span, not a live hot-streak call, and it is box-composite only, not an adjusted impact metric.

entries.q: How does LeBron James still look efficient this deep into his career?

a.answer: Across the 3-season sample LeBron shot 52.3 percent from the field while averaging 24.8 points and 8.3 assists per 36 minutes over 201 games -- a rich field-goal mark for a perimeter creator carrying a heavy playmaking load. Free throws are the soft spot at 75.6 percent, the weakest number in an otherwise efficient line. The rate says nothing about how those minutes were used or against whom.

entries.q: What is the catch with Joel Embiid's numbers?

a.answer: When on the floor Embiid is dominant -- 33.3 points and 10.3 rebounds per 36 minutes, plus a guard-like 87.4 percent from the line for a center. The headline caveat is availability: just 93 games and 2,977.5 minutes over three seasons, a smaller sample than most stars here. Per-36 rates do not reflect that missed availability.

entries.q: How much has Ja Morant actually played over this window?

a.answer: Ja dishes 9.0 assists and scores 26.6 points per 36 minutes, among the top guard playmaking rates in this pack -- but he appears in just 79 games and 2,405.0 minutes over the sample, the smallest game count here. His three-point touch is a weak spot at 29.0 percent. With only 79 games the rate line rests on the thinnest sample in the group.

entries.q: How has James Harden's role changed?
alt_phrasings: Is Harden more of a passer now?

a.answer: Harden's role has shifted toward setup: 8.7 assists per 36 minutes against a 21.7-point scoring rate, and he logs the largest game count in this pack at 219. His 42.4 percent field-goal mark reflects a heavy three-point and drawn-foul diet the raw rate does not separate, and he stays reliable at the line at 87.7 percent. The game-count comparison is only against the 20 stars in this pack.

entries.q: Is Kawhi Leonard still a three-level scorer?

a.answer: Kawhi's shooting line is 51.1 / 40.4 / 87.9 from the field, three, and the line -- efficient in every zone -- while scoring 27.1 points per 36 minutes over 164 games. His assist rate is low at 3.8 per 36, a scorer more than a distributor. Shooting percentages are unadjusted for shot difficulty.

entries.q: How does Anthony Edwards combine scoring and range?

a.answer: Edwards logs 27.7 points per 36 minutes with real range at 38.6 percent from three, and he is durable -- 217 games and 7,730.4 minutes in the window, backed by an 82.4 percent free-throw mark. Minutes and games speak to availability, not to how efficiently those minutes were used. All figures are per-36 rates over three seasons.

entries.q: What is Anthony Davis's statistical identity?
alt_phrasings: Is Anthony Davis a floor spacer?

a.answer: Davis posts a true two-way big line -- 25.4 points and 12.7 rebounds per 36 minutes on strong 53.5 percent interior shooting. The floor-spacing is limited, with a 27.6 percent three-point mark that reflects a low-volume, interior-focused shot profile. These are per-36 rates over three seasons, unadjusted for role or opponent.

entries.q: Where is Zion Williamson elite and where is he weak?

a.answer: Zion's interior scoring is elite -- 26.9 points per 36 minutes on 58.0 percent from the field -- but the free-throw line is a clear weak point at 69.6 percent, and his 28.6 percent three-point mark shows the range is limited. He appears in 157 games across the three-season window. The high field-goal rate reflects a rim-heavy shot diet.

entries.q: Is Jimmy Butler a high-volume scorer?

a.answer: Butler's scoring is efficient rather than high-volume: 21.5 points per 36 minutes on 50.6 percent shooting, plus 6.0 rebounds and 5.7 assists per 36 across 152 games and an 85.5 percent free-throw mark. A lower per-36 scoring rate reflects role and shot volume, not necessarily lower impact.

entries.q: What is Kyrie Irving's efficiency like?

a.answer: Kyrie's efficiency is guard-elite: 40.6 percent from three and 91.0 percent at the free-throw line, on a 25.6-points-per-36 rate and 48.6 percent overall shooting. His window here spans two seasons and 108 games, a smaller sample than the three-season stars. Numbers are per-36 rates, unadjusted for shot difficulty.

entries.q: How good is Damian Lillard at the free-throw line?

a.answer: Lillard's 92.1 percent free-throw mark is among the best in this pack of stars, and he blends scoring and playmaking at 24.8 points and 7.1 assists per 36 minutes. His overall 43.5 percent field-goal rate is consistent with a deep-range, high-volume shot diet. The two-season window is a smaller sample than most.

entries.q: Is Devin Booker just a scorer, or does he create too?

a.answer: Booker is a scorer who also runs offense: 26.5 points and 6.8 assists per 36 minutes, and he is excellent at the line at 88.4 percent. Durability is a plus with 207 games and 7,387.8 minutes in the window, while his 34.1 percent three-point efficiency is unadjusted for shot mix.

entries.q: What is Jayson Tatum's box profile?
alt_phrasings: Is Tatum a good three-point shooter?

a.answer: Tatum is a wing scorer who also rebounds -- 26.5 points and 8.6 rebounds per 36 minutes over 162 games -- and he gets to the line and converts at 82.4 percent. His three-point efficiency is average at 35.5 percent, a volume-over-touch profile from deep. Numbers are per-36 rates unadjusted for shot difficulty.

entries.q: How much is Jokic worth to Denver in win probability?
alt_phrasings: What happens to the Nuggets without Jokic?

a.answer: On a neutral floor against a league-average team, mapping Denver's on/off swing onto the Elo win-prob curve drops the Nuggets from 0.634 with Jokic to 0.0517 without -- a 0.5822 swing, the largest of any team's top on/off player. That figure is a ceiling, not a clean player value: it attributes a full-lineup on-vs-off gap to one man, with no control for teammates, opponent, or garbage time. It is descriptive, not a betting number.

entries.q: How does OKC's win probability change with and without SGA?

a.answer: On a neutral floor versus a league-average opponent, the star-removal exercise moves OKC from 0.7829 with Shai Gilgeous-Alexander to 0.2658 without -- a 0.5171 win-prob swing. Like every row in this exhibit it is a ceiling built from an on/off net-rating delta, a roster confound rather than a controlled individual value, and it is descriptive only.

entries.q: Why is the biggest on/off player on some teams a role player and not the star?
alt_phrasings: Why isn't Curry Golden State's top on/off guy?
Why is Luke Kornet ahead of Tatum on Boston?
Is on/off a good measure of stars?

a.answer: Because raw on/off is a full-lineup swing, not an individual-value estimate, it often flatters bench-anchoring role players: the exhibit's top on/off name is Luke Kornet on Boston (0.2785 swing), Gui Santos on Golden State (0.2378), Dorian Finney-Smith on the Lakers (0.4656), Monte Morris in Phoenix (0.2593), and Isaac Okoro in Cleveland (0.303) -- not Tatum, Curry, LeBron, Booker, or Mitchell. Floor-sharing correlates with coach trust, opponent strength, and garbage-time minutes, none of which are controlled. Treat a big on/off number as a flag to investigate, not a verdict.

entries.q: Does a huge on/off number really mean a player is that valuable?
alt_phrasings: How big are most on/off numbers?

a.answer: The stars separate hard at the top -- Victor Wembanyama led the 2025-26 slice at +17.043 per 48 and Jokic was +23.713 the season before -- but the median qualified player sits at just +0.127, so most on/off gaps are noise around zero. That near-zero median is the guardrail: a big on/off figure is rare and easy to misread, because who a player shares the floor with is tangled up with opponent strength and garbage time. It is descriptive only until an earned predictive receipt says otherwise.

entries.q: Which players top a simple box-score value index?
alt_phrasings: Who ranks highest on raw box production?

a.answer: A frozen, untuned box-score value index puts Nikola Jokic on top at 30.86 points of value per 36 minutes, ahead of Giannis Antetokounmpo (27.558) and Victor Wembanyama (26.261), pooled over 77,744 rows and ranking the 501 players past the 750-minute floor. Recovering the consensus star order from weights fixed in advance is a sanity check on the box-score data, not a claim to reproduce RAPM, EPM, or BPM. Accented names split across two IDs upstream, so Jokic can appear twice in the top rows.

entries.q: Which team scored the most per game in the latest season of the sample?
alt_phrasings: Who put up the most points per game?

a.answer: Denver posted the highest latest-season scoring in the sample at 121.4 points per game, and Nikola Jokic anchors the roster at 51.2 points-plus-rebounds-plus-assists per 36 minutes -- the top such contributor rate across all 30 teams. ppg is a single-season team average while the rest of the sample spans three seasons, and PRA-per-36 is a raw box rate, not an impact metric.

entries.q: Which team played at the fastest pace?

a.answer: By the pace proxy in the latest season, Miami is the fastest at 105.8, and it also scored 120.4 points per game with Bam Adebayo as its most-used player at a 35.2 PRA-per-36 rate. Pace_proxy is a proxy, not official possession-based pace, and the manifest is descriptive with no schedule or opponent adjustment.

entries.q: Which team played at the slowest pace?

a.answer: Boston played at the lowest pace proxy in the sample at 97.5 while still scoring 114.9 points per game in the latest season. A quirk of the data: the Celtics' most-used player by total minutes is Derrick White at 7,576.2, a reminder the minutes leader is not always the marquee name. Pace_proxy is a proxy, not official pace, and top-contributor is a minutes ranking, not a best-player ranking.

entries.q: Who logged the most minutes for Golden State -- surely Curry?
alt_phrasings: Is Curry the Warriors' minutes leader?

a.answer: No -- the Warriors' most-used player by total minutes across the 3-season sample is Brandin Podziemski at 6,018.4 minutes, a young wing, not Stephen Curry. His combined PRA-per-36 is 27.1, and the team scored 114.6 points per game at a 101.7 pace proxy. The 'top contributor' is a minutes ranking, so a high-minutes role player can outrank a star with heavier per-game impact but fewer minutes.

entries.q: Who is the Lakers' most-used player and what is his rate?

a.answer: The Lakers' most-used player by total minutes is LeBron James at 6,940.9 minutes, posting a 40.5 combined PRA-per-36 rate, and the team scored 116.3 points per game at a middle-of-the-pack 99.8 pace proxy. PRA-per-36 is a raw box rate, not an impact metric, and ppg is a single-season figure.

entries.q: How dominant is SGA's box production for the Thunder?

a.answer: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander leads Oklahoma City at 45.4 points-plus-rebounds-plus-assists per 36 minutes across 245 team-games, one of the highest top-contributor rates in the sample, and he is also the minutes leader at 7,375.7. The team scored 119.0 points per game in the latest season. PRA-per-36 is a box rate, not an impact metric.

entries.q: Which team scored the fewest points per game?

a.answer: In the latest season of the sample Brooklyn scored the fewest at 106.2 points per game, with Nic Claxton its most-used player at a 28.2 PRA-per-36 rate. ppg here is a single-season team average, descriptive with no opponent or schedule adjustment.

entries.q: How much does Milwaukee's box production run through Giannis?

a.answer: Giannis Antetokounmpo leads Milwaukee at 50.9 points-plus-rebounds-plus-assists per 36 minutes -- one of the two highest top-contributor rates in the sample alongside Jokic -- while the Bucks scored 109.3 points per game at a 98.4 pace proxy. That team scoring is on the low end of the league; PRA-per-36 is a box rate, not an impact metric.

entries.q: Who carries Cleveland's box production?

a.answer: Donovan Mitchell is Cleveland's most-used player at a 39.3 PRA-per-36 rate over 6,482.5 minutes, and the Cavaliers scored 119.6 points per game at a 102.1 pace proxy in the latest season. PRA-per-36 sums points, rebounds, and assists per 36 minutes as a raw box rate, not a measured impact number.

entries.q: What does Cade Cunningham's box rate look like for Detroit?

a.answer: Cade Cunningham leads Detroit at a 40.6 PRA-per-36 rate over 6,622.9 minutes, and the Pistons scored 117.4 points per game at a 102.5 pace proxy. It is a raw box rate over the 3-season sample, not adjusted for opponent or role.

entries.q: How much does New York run through Jalen Brunson?

a.answer: Jalen Brunson is the Knicks' most-used player at a 37.9 PRA-per-36 rate over 7,566.2 minutes, and New York scored 115.7 points per game at a slow 98.2 pace proxy. PRA-per-36 is a box rate, descriptive only, with no schedule or opponent adjustment.

entries.q: How big is home-court advantage in the box score?
alt_phrasings: How much do home teams shoot better?

a.answer: Pooled over 74,450 player-games, the home edge is small and lives mostly in shooting: home teams shoot 47.479 percent from the field versus 46.833 on the road (+0.647 points) and 36.632 versus 35.867 from three (+0.765), while the typical player's home-minus-away scoring gap is just +0.04 points per game. It is a faint, league-wide tilt, not the outsized boost fans assume. Descriptive only.

entries.q: Does playing on the second night of a back-to-back hurt production?
alt_phrasings: Do players slump on no rest?
How much does a back-to-back cost?

a.answer: Fatigue shows up modestly at the player level: on the second night of a back-to-back, per-36 box-composite production dips about 0.315 versus rested games (13.591 vs 13.905), with smaller dips for 3-games-in-4 and 4-in-6. A significance-tested team version puts it at -1.73 points per 100 possessions of offensive rating (rested minus back-to-back, n=4732, p=0.0056). The player-level figure is descriptive and not opponent- or minutes-adjusted.

entries.q: How much does a player's shooting swing with matchup, venue, and rest?
alt_phrasings: Does defense tier move efficiency much?
How streaky is shooting by context?

a.answer: Very little. Of the 50 highest-minute players, the most context-sensitive shooter is Payton Pritchard, whose True Shooting percentage swings by only about 4.4 points on average across defense tier, venue, and rest, with his biggest single split being +6.0 TS points on the second night of a back-to-back. Most of the top 50 sit lower, so efficiency is far stickier across context than road-warrior narratives suggest. Cells below 10 player-games are dropped, and it is raw split dispersion, not a causal claim.

entries.q: Which recurring matchup produces the most points, and which the fewest?
alt_phrasings: Which head-to-head goes over the most?

a.answer: Pooled over three seasons and 870 team pairings, Atlanta versus Indiana is the highest-scoring matchup at a mean of 255.7 combined points over 10 meetings, while Charlotte versus Portland is the lowest at 197.0 -- a 58-point gap between the league's fastest and slowest recurring games. This describes games already played, not a forecast of any future meeting, and it is not a home/away split.

entries.q: Does slowing the game down really help the underdog?
alt_phrasings: Does pace help the weaker team?
How much does tempo change upset odds?

a.answer: It helps, but only a little. Across the NBA's observed pace range of about 92 to 104 possessions, an 80 percent favorite's upset probability rises only from 19.5 percent at the fastest pace to 20.9 percent at the slowest -- a 1.4-point swing. Fewer possessions mean fewer chances for the better team to separate, but real NBA pace barely moves game to game, so the mechanical effect on any single matchup is small. This isolates the variance mechanism only, holding per-possession scoring fixed.

entries.q: How much does the Pelicans' win probability move with and without Zion?
alt_phrasings: New Orleans with and without Zion

a.answer: In the star-removal exhibit, New Orleans moves from 0.3292 with Zion Williamson to 0.0469 without on a neutral floor versus a league-average team -- a 0.2823 swing, off a low starting team strength. It is a ceiling built from an on/off net-rating delta with a roster confound, descriptive only, not a betting number.

entries.q: What is Wembanyama's star value to San Antonio in this exhibit?

a.answer: San Antonio moves from 0.3901 with Victor Wembanyama to 0.112 without on a neutral floor against a league-average opponent -- a 0.2781 win-prob swing. As with every row, it is a ceiling from a roster-confounded on/off delta, not a controlled individual value, and it is descriptive rather than an edge claim.

entries.q: Does the system know when a late-game lead is basically safe?
alt_phrasings: Is the win-prob model calibrated late in games?
How well does it read game state?

a.answer: In the bulk of regulation states it tracks reality closely: for a 1-to-5 point lead with 24-36 minutes left, the model's mean win probability is 0.6204 across 898 games and teams in that state actually won 62.03 percent of the time. The honest exception is overtime -- with a 1-5 lead in OT the model says 0.7113 while teams actually won 98.3 percent and the market priced 97.6 percent, so it under-rates how decisive a late lead is and the market is better there. This is a calibration exhibit, never a profit claim.

entries.q: Can you give me Jokic's clutch or fourth-quarter splits?
alt_phrasings: How does Jokic play in the clutch?
Fourth quarter per-36 for a player

a.answer: Not from this data. The NBA boxscores table is a full-game aggregate with no period or clutch grain, so a Q4 or overtime per-36 split cannot be computed without fabricating it -- and the module refuses rather than invent one. The per-period box lines do exist in the raw cache, but the ingest step sums them into one full-game row and discards the period grain, so recovering clutch splits is a data-layer re-ingest that is out of scope here.

entries.q: Which teams are best at protecting leads versus storming back?
alt_phrasings: Who holds leads and who rallies?

a.answer: A per-team front-runner-versus-comeback profile is not buildable from this slice: zero of 30 teams clear the floor of at least two games both leading and trailing at halftime in the 26-game corpus, so per-team labels would be 1-2 game noise. The only robust readout is league-level -- second-half margin regresses on halftime margin with a slope of 0.2885, and a team that led at half went on to a +1.346 second-half margin on average. The module declines to print per-team rankings rather than over-claim.

entries.q: Can you give me a player's aging curve or age-adjusted projection?
alt_phrasings: What does the aging curve say?
Is this player past his prime by the model?

a.answer: Aging curves are not buildable from this data. No birthdate or age column exists in any NBA table, and only three season snapshots (2023-24, 2024-25, 2025-26) are on hand, while aging-curve methods need age-labeled player-seasons across many seasons. The codebase's own audit reaches the same defer verdict; add age labels and more seasons and it becomes testable.

entries.q: What is this player's RAPM, EPM, or DARKO?
alt_phrasings: Give me an impact metric like EPM
What does DARKO say about him?

a.answer: Those are not reproduced. From 77,744 box-score rows the system can honestly build a box-only value index, per-36 rates, and unadjusted on/off, but RAPM, xRAPM, EPM, DARKO, LEBRON, BPM, and RAPTOR are all marked do-not-fake because the required league-wide RAPM target or continuous tracking inputs do not exist in the repo. Support means raw input-column coverage only, never a claim to reproduce a branded metric under a borrowed name.

entries.q: Can you rank every NBA team by true offensive rating or possessions?
alt_phrasings: Give me real pace and ORtg per team

a.answer: Not at that grain from the team manifest. The team cards carry ppg_latest_season and a pace_proxy, but pace_proxy is explicitly a proxy, not official possession-based pace, and ppg is a single-season average with no schedule or opponent adjustment. A true possession-based offensive rating and official pace are not what this descriptive manifest provides, so ranking teams by them here would overstate what the data supports.

entries.q: Is Jokic's 0.58 win-probability swing a clean measure of his individual value?
alt_phrasings: Can I trust the with/without win prob as player value?
Does star removal isolate one player?

a.answer: No -- it is explicitly a ceiling, not a clean causal player value. The 0.5822 swing comes from attributing a full-lineup on-vs-off net-rating gap to one man, with no control for teammates, opponent, coach trust, or garbage time, and the net-rating-to-Elo conversion is a single frozen constant, not a fit. It is a comparable, honest price tag on star dependence, useful as matchup context but labeled descriptive-only, not an edge or a true individual-value estimate.

entries.q: Does Giannis's high field-goal percentage mean he is a great shooter?
alt_phrasings: Is Giannis a good shooter because of 60 percent FG?
What does Giannis's 60.9 percent really mean?

a.answer: Not in the way it sounds -- his 60.9 percent from the field largely reflects a rim-heavy shot diet, not touch from range. The range and line numbers tell the other half: 27.4 percent from three and 64.0 percent on free throws. So the elite field-goal rate is about where the shots come from, which the raw percentage does not separate from shooting skill.

entries.q: Between Luka and Jokic, who is the steadier producer?
alt_phrasings: Who is more metronomic, Luka or Jokic?
Compare Doncic and Jokic game-to-game variance

a.answer: They are essentially tied at the top, with Luka Doncic just ahead: a shrunk composite coefficient of variation of 0.3448 for Doncic versus 0.3456 for Jokic, both far under the league median of 0.6235 among 579 players. Their nightly production barely wobbles, roughly half the game-to-game variability of a median rotation player. Lower CV means steadier, not necessarily more valuable, and no opponent or rest adjustment is applied.

entries.q: How much does Milwaukee's win probability depend on Giannis in the star-removal exhibit?

a.answer: Milwaukee moves from 0.6059 with Giannis Antetokounmpo to 0.1617 without on a neutral floor versus a league-average team -- a 0.4441 win-prob swing, among the largest for a team's clear lead star. Like every row it is a ceiling from a roster-confounded on/off delta, descriptive and not a causal or betting number.

entries.q: Which is the more reliable star profile, Kawhi Leonard or Kevin Durant on efficiency?
alt_phrasings: Who shoots better across zones, Kawhi or Durant?

a.answer: Both are three-level shooters with nearly matched lines: Kawhi at 51.1 / 40.4 / 87.9 and Durant at 52.3 / 41.8 / 85.8 from the field, three, and the line. Kawhi scores 27.1 points per 36 to Durant's 26.0, and both are low-assist, score-first roles (3.8 and 4.6 assists per 36). These are per-36 rates unadjusted for shot difficulty, so treat them as efficiency profiles, not a ranking of impact.

entries.q: Who is the biggest faller in form over the sample?
alt_phrasings: Which player trended down the most?
Who lost the most box production?

a.answer: Myles Turner is the biggest faller, with his 10-game rolling per-36 box composite down -11.043 over the observed span -- the mirror image of Wembanyama's league-leading +19.821 rise to 37.869. This is a net change over the whole multi-season span, a trajectory read rather than a current streak, and it is box-composite only, not age- or opponent-adjusted.

entries.q: How many players and games sit behind these NBA player numbers?
alt_phrasings: What is the data coverage for player metrics?
How big is the box-score sample?
How many rows feed the player analytics?

a.answer: The box-score layer covers 77,744 player-game rows spanning 807 unique players and 3,611 games, with full box scores at zero percent missing. That coverage supports box-only value, per-36 rates, and unadjusted on/off, but it is the reason branded impact metrics are declined -- the raw inputs for RAPM or continuous tracking are not present. Coverage means input-column completeness, not a claim about any adjusted metric.

entries.q: Is the atlas 'top contributor' the same as a team's best player?
alt_phrasings: Does top contributor mean best player?
What does top contributor actually measure?
Why is a role player listed as top contributor?

a.answer: No -- the 'top contributor' is simply the player with the most total minutes for a team across the sample, not the best or highest-scoring one. That is why Boston's is Derrick White (7,576.2 minutes) and Golden State's is Brandin Podziemski (6,018.4), not the marquee names, while on Denver and Oklahoma City it happens to coincide with the lead star. The metric alongside it, PRA-per-36, is a raw box rate, not an impact measure.

entries.q: What can you show me?

a.answer: Five surfaces. /analytics/forecaster is the calibration proof for the prediction engine; /analytics/the-loop shows how a claim is proposed, tested and killed; /analytics/browse opens all 54 analysis modules; /analytics/players opens 1,549 entity cards across seven packs; and /analytics/explainers is the plain-language layer. The retraction story sits at /analytics/findings/retraction.

entries.q: Where do I start?
alt_phrasings: what should I look at first

a.answer: Start at /analytics/forecaster if you want to know whether the predictions are any good, or /analytics/the-loop if you want to know how the system decides what to believe. Both are short, both end in a number you can trace to a committed artifact, and both are honest about where the model loses.

entries.q: What can you show me about how good the predictions are?

a.answer: /analytics/forecaster assembles six committed aggregates: walk-forward win-probability results, state-conditioned calibration, the Murphy decomposition, calibration stability, Brier skill scores and the cross-sport scoreboard. The headline it supports is calibration, not profit -- the model matches the devigged close pregame and trails the market in-game.

entries.q: What can you show me about how the system works?

a.answer: /analytics/the-loop walks the cycle from claim to verdict: propose, gate, record, retract. The ledgers behind it are public too -- 287 tested mechanisms at /analytics/m/mechanism_survival and /analytics/m/fwd_claim_scoreboard, and the failures at /analytics/m/reject_graveyard.

entries.q: What can you show me about failed signals?

a.answer: /analytics/m/reject_graveyard holds 804 recorded verdict rows, 68 distinct signals currently sitting on a REJECT-family verdict, and the reason categories behind them. The explainer at /analytics/explainers/the-graveyard makes the case for why publishing failures is the point.

entries.q: What can you show me about a specific NBA player?

a.answer: /analytics/players is the atlas front door, and NBA players live under /analytics/players/nba_players/<slug>. The pack holds 482 players who clear a floor of 800 career minutes out of 807 eligible. Each card is a descriptive career summary -- per-36 rates, shooting percentages, games and minutes -- not a projection.

entries.q: What can you show me about NBA teams?

a.answer: Team cards are their own atlas pack under /analytics/players/nba_teams/<slug>. For team-level analysis rather than cards, /analytics/m/ctx_team_states, /analytics/m/nba_matchup_grid and /analytics/m/home_away_anatomy are the relevant modules.

entries.q: What can you show me about baseball?
alt_phrasings: what do you have on mlb

a.answer: The deepest sport here. /analytics/m/mlb_count_leverage and /analytics/m/pitch_sequencing cover 693,037 pitches from the 2025 Statcast pull; /analytics/m/mlb_velo_bands and /analytics/m/statcast_showcase cover the pitch-level detail; and batters and pitch types have their own atlas packs at /analytics/players/mlb_batters and /analytics/players/mlb_pitch.

entries.q: What can you show me about soccer?
alt_phrasings: what do you have on soccer

a.answer: /analytics/m/soccer_calibration_pack and /analytics/m/soccer_form_stability are the two dedicated modules, and soccer teams have an atlas pack at /analytics/players/soccer. Be aware of the sample: the graded in-game soccer corpus is 9,003 rows against MLB's 78,986, and the model's Brier skill versus the market there is -0.5967.

entries.q: What can you show me about tennis?
alt_phrasings: what do you have on tennis

a.answer: /analytics/m/tennis_showcase and /analytics/m/tennis_surface_transfer, plus a tennis atlas pack at /analytics/players/tennis. Tennis is the thinnest sport on market structure: no reliability map, so /analytics/m/xsport_structure records it not_buildable rather than estimating.

entries.q: What can you show me about calibration?

a.answer: Four modules and an explainer. /analytics/m/calibration_by_market_type splits it by market, /analytics/m/calibration_over_time and /analytics/m/calibration_stability cover drift, /analytics/m/state_conditioned_calibration conditions on game state, and /analytics/explainers/what-calibration-means explains why the market is the benchmark. Calibration checkpoints also have their own atlas pack at /analytics/players/calibration.

entries.q: What can you show me about the model versus the market?
alt_phrasings: head to head with the market
where do you compare to the odds

a.answer: /analytics/m/cross_sport_scoreboard carries the 17 paired head-to-head rows with sample sizes, confidence intervals and verdicts; /analytics/m/brier_skill_scores gives the skill-score view; and /analytics/m/kernel_transfer explains which comparisons are even legitimate across sports. All three are stamped edge_claimed=false.

entries.q: What can you show me about how betting lines move?

a.answer: Four modules: /analytics/m/micro_absorption for how motion distributes across the pre-game window, /analytics/m/micro_closing_decay for the run-up to close, /analytics/m/tick_microstructure for tick-level behavior and /analytics/m/market_convergence for how prices tighten in-game. The Line Half-Life stat sits on top of the first of these.

entries.q: What can you show me about market overreaction?

a.answer: /analytics/m/market_overreaction measures the overshoot and /analytics/m/market_disagreement_profile measures who is right when the model and market disagree. Read them together: the overshoot is real, and at maximum disagreement the model is the closer of the two only 37.73% of the time in MLB and 21.52% in soccer.

entries.q: What can you show me about schedule and rest?

a.answer: /analytics/m/schedule_density holds the back-to-back, 3-in-4 and 4-in-6 congestion counts across 90 team-seasons, and it is the sole input to the Schedule Fatigue Tax. The underlying effect is a recorded CONFIRMED_LOCAL mechanism: -1.73 pts/100 team ORtg, n=4,732, p=0.0056.

entries.q: What can you show me about what happens when a star sits?

a.answer: Two modules that disagree with each other, which is the interesting part: /analytics/m/cf_star_removal is the Elo on/off counterfactual and /analytics/m/ctx_lineup_proxy is the raw with/without split. Across 30 teams they name the same most-indispensable player only once, at an agree rate of 0.0333. /analytics/m/on_off_showcase covers the underlying on/off data.

entries.q: What can you show me about blowouts and comebacks?

a.answer: /analytics/m/blowout_dynamics finds the point of no return from the score path alone, and /analytics/m/comeback_atlas catalogs the comebacks themselves. The market-side companion is /analytics/m/xsport_structure, where NBA favorites past a 0.85 in-game price hold 98.54% of the time across 5,578 games.

entries.q: What can you show me about clutch performance?

a.answer: /analytics/m/clutch_context is the module, and it is context-conditioned rather than a raw late-game split. Pair it with /analytics/m/ctx_player_splits and /analytics/m/nba_consistency_profiles if you want the same player viewed through different context axes.

entries.q: What can you show me about player aging?

a.answer: /analytics/m/aging_curve_lite, which is deliberately labeled 'lite' -- it is a descriptive curve over the local boxscore corpus, not a projection system. /analytics/m/player_metric_landscape and /analytics/m/box_value_index cover the broader player-metric surface.

entries.q: What can you show me about the computer vision work?

a.answer: /analytics/m/cv_tracking_stats is the committed summary of the tracking pipeline's output. It is a measurement artifact from the vision layer, not a live video feed, and the analytics on this site do not depend on it.

entries.q: What can you show me about the retraction?

a.answer: /analytics/findings/retraction is the full account of the numbers that were withdrawn and why. The claim ledger backs it up: 7 claim families currently sit on a retracted status, 6 of them MLB.

entries.q: What can you show me about who built this?

a.answer: /analytics/about covers the project and the person directing it, and /analytics/m/agent_fleet_history has the numbers: 3,224 commits between 2026-03-09 and 2026-07-22, 95.75% agent-authored. The narrative version is at /analytics/explainers/how-ai-agents-built-this.

entries.q: What can you show me about the simulator?

a.answer: /analytics/explainers/how-a-possession-simulator-thinks is the plain-language walkthrough of how possession-level simulation produces a distribution rather than a single number. The scored output of that machinery is what /analytics/forecaster grades.

entries.q: What explainers are available?

a.answer: Six, at /analytics/explainers: how a possession simulator thinks, what calibration means and why we grade against the market, the graveyard and why we publish what failed, how AI agents built this and what a human decided, reading an entity card without fooling yourself, and what the Ask AI can and cannot tell you.

entries.q: How do I read an entity card properly?
alt_phrasings: how to read a player card

a.answer: /analytics/explainers/reading-an-entity-card is written for exactly that. The short version: the cards are descriptive career summaries behind declared floors -- NBA players need 800 career minutes, which admits 482 of 807 -- and nothing on them is a forecast.

entries.q: What can this Ask feature actually do?

a.answer: It answers from committed artifacts only, and returns one of five statuses -- ok, no_data, not_supported, ambiguous or refused -- with a source artifact and an as-of date on anything it does answer. /analytics/explainers/what-the-ask-ai-can-and-cannot-tell-you is the honest scope statement; the coverage numbers are at /analytics/m/qa_coverage_stats.

entries.q: Where do I find a specific module?

a.answer: /analytics/browse lists all 54 modules, and each one opens at /analytics/m/<id> where the id is the module name -- /analytics/m/murphy_decomposition, /analytics/m/residual_anatomy, /analytics/m/why_attribution and so on. Every module page carries its own source path, floors and as-of.

entries.q: What can you show me about how many claims you've tested?

a.answer: /analytics/m/mechanism_survival and /analytics/m/fwd_claim_scoreboard between them cover 287 tested mechanisms and 259 claim families -- 121 verified, 99 null, 28 not-testable, 7 retracted and 4 provisional. /analytics/m/honesty_exhibit is the summary view, where nulls outnumber confirms 2.1 to 1.

entries.q: What can you show me about the size of the knowledge base?

a.answer: /analytics/m/claims_corpus_meta has the counts: 103 claim families and 103,048 generated claims, with 98.85% covered by a validation sample and 0 mismatches. /analytics/m/dossier_completeness covers how complete the per-entity dossiers are.

entries.q: What can you show me about where the model goes wrong?

a.answer: Three modules aimed squarely at that: /analytics/m/residual_anatomy dissects the errors, /analytics/m/residual_autocorrelation checks whether they cluster, and /analytics/m/why_attribution attributes them. /analytics/m/murphy_decomposition then splits the gap into miscalibration versus missing information.

entries.q: What can you show me about paper trading?

a.answer: /analytics/m/paper_execution_audit is an execution-quality measurement -- how orders would have filled and how state lag affects that -- not a returns ledger. No profit, ROI or bankroll figure is published anywhere on this site, and questions phrased that way are refused rather than answered.

entries.q: What can you show me about league parity?

a.answer: /analytics/m/league_parity_index, covering three NBA seasons and 3,611 games with win-share Gini, HHI, win-percentage dispersion and margin dispersion. The most balanced season measured is 2023-24 at a Gini of 0.177; the least is 2025-26 at 0.2004.

entries.q: What can you show me about in-game information arrival?

a.answer: /analytics/m/info_arrival_curve pairs model, market and naive Brier by game time, and /analytics/m/market_convergence tracks how the price tightens. Together they are the input to the Market Foresight Premium, which finds the market's per-bit advantage rising through the game in both sports measured.

entries.q: What can you show me about form and momentum?

a.answer: /analytics/m/nba_form_curves and /analytics/m/soccer_form_stability are the two form modules. Bear in mind the gate result before reading them as signals: every form candidate tested against the devigged close was rejected across independent corpora.

entries.q: What can you show me about counterfactuals?

a.answer: /analytics/m/cf_star_removal simulates a team without its most important player and /analytics/m/cf_pace_variance varies pace. Both are counterfactuals over a model, so they inherit the model's assumptions -- the star-removal one explicitly carries a roster confound and is not a causal impact estimate.

entries.q: Can you show me tonight's games or predictions?

a.answer: No. There is no live schedule, live odds or live game-state feed behind this site -- every page reads committed artifacts from completed games. What exists instead is the graded record: /analytics/forecaster for how the predictions scored, and /analytics/m/cross_sport_scoreboard for the head-to-head against the market.

entries.q: Can you show me which bets to make?

a.answer: No. This is a calibration product and every module carries edge_claimed=false; no pick, stake, ROI or bankroll figure is published anywhere. If you want the honest reason, /analytics/m/cross_sport_scoreboard and /analytics/m/brier_skill_scores show the model trailing the market at every in-game grain measured.

entries.q: Is there a page comparing the sports directly?

a.answer: Two. /analytics/m/xsport_structure applies one reliability methodology across sports and honestly records three of four as not_buildable, and /analytics/m/kernel_transfer states which cross-sport axes are legitimate at all -- the Murphy reliability component is comparable, CRPS on run totals is not.

entries.q: Where can I see the raw numbers behind a chart?

a.answer: On the module page itself. Each of the 54 entries in the manifest records its output path, chart path, status, edge_claimed flag and as-of, so /analytics/m/<id> can name the exact artifact a number came from. Modules whose computation does not stamp a date record a null as-of rather than inventing one.

entries.q: Which modules are incomplete?

a.answer: The manifest flags them by status rather than hiding them -- blowout_dynamics, for instance, is marked partial. Aggregate health is published too: 63 of 63 checks green at build time, with per-module pass status and timing in the check report.

entries.q: What's the most interesting thing on this site?

a.answer: Subjectively, the parts where the system argues against itself. /analytics/m/reject_graveyard has 804 recorded verdicts against 95 SHIPs; /analytics/m/honesty_exhibit reports nulls outnumbering confirms 2.1 to 1; and the Overreaction Harvest Gap measures a real market overshoot and then records that the model cannot harvest it. Those are harder to fake than a leaderboard.

entries.q: Is there anything here about hockey or football?

a.answer: No. The covered sports are NBA, MLB, soccer and tennis, with WNBA appearing only in the line-movement measurement. There are no NFL or NHL corpora behind this site, so there is nothing to show rather than something thin.

entries.q: How does this system grade itself?
alt_phrasings: how do you check your own work

a.answer: Every named mechanism the system tests is written to an append-only validation ledger with its verdict, effect size, p-value, and the corpus it ran on. The scoreboard over those ledgers currently counts 287 rows across four sports, of which 129 of 256 testable hypotheses survived as confirmed -- a survival rate of 0.5039. A confirmed, a null, and a not-testable are all recorded and counted; a system that only ever confirmed would not be credible.

entries.q: How many of your claims are verified versus null?

a.answer: In the forward claim scoreboard over 259 hypothesis families, 121 are verified, 99 are null, 28 not-testable, 7 retracted, and 4 provisional. That is a ratio of 1.107 nulls-or-worse per confirm. The nulls are kept and published on purpose -- they are the honest shape of a real search, not a defect.

entries.q: Do nulls actually outnumber your confirmed findings?
alt_phrasings: how many things did not work

a.answer: Yes. Across the four sport ledgers plus a 1,003-row interaction-factory sweep, nulls (351) outnumber confirms (168) by about 2.1x. In MLB the balance actually inverts, 32 confirmed against 37 null. Keeping the failures visible is the entire point of the exhibit.

entries.q: What was the biggest result you had to retract?
alt_phrasings: a headline number that fell apart

a.answer: The most-cited retraction was an early pregame return-on-investment headline that turned out to be a market-follow grading artifact: the grader picked bet direction from the market's own devigged favorite and never actually read the model, priced at a flat -110 fiction, with filters tuned in-sample on the same file. Read against real closing lines the model is roughly break-even-minus-vig, about -2.00% unfiltered. The instrument that caught it was built by the same person who made the claim.

entries.q: Tell me about the in-play backtest headline you pulled back.

a.answer: An in-play backtest once posted eye-catching accuracy and return figures on 55,073 bets, but those were settled against a soft L5 rolling-average line proxy, not real sharp closing lines. That makes it a model-quality ceiling, not a tradeable or realized result, so both figures were retracted and no dollar number is quoted in their place. The first real closing-line-value reading is not expected until October 2026.

entries.q: Did you find a leak in your own win-probability model?
alt_phrasings: did a feature peek at the future

a.answer: Yes. The end-of-third-quarter win-probability model was fed two features computed from fourth-quarter data (halftime_pace_shift and trailing_team_q4_usg_hhi), so it was peeking at the quarter it was supposed to predict, and the famous Brier headline was also mis-sourced from the cited file. After removing the two leaking features the honest leak-free walk-forward Brier is about 0.141. It is framed as a leak caught in my own pipeline, not as a competitive number.

entries.q: How big is the reject pile?
alt_phrasings: how many signals did you kill

a.answer: The reject ledger holds 804 recorded verdict rows, of which 628 are on a REJECT-family verdict (627 explicit REJECT) against 95 SHIP and 45 SHIP_REVIEW. As of their latest test, 68 distinct sport-signal pairs currently sit on a reject verdict. A REJECT is honest market-efficiency evidence, not a failure -- no dollar or edge claim rides on any of it.

entries.q: Why do you reject so many signals?
alt_phrasings: most common reason for a reject
why does the gate kill candidates

a.answer: By reason category, the largest bucket of rejects is the as-of reclaim sweep at 510, followed by prescreen-delta (20), walk-forward ablation (18), and seed-stability (17). By sport the reject rows split NBA 426, soccer 205, MLB 118, tennis 55. Most candidates simply do not clear a leak-free gate that was built to refute, not confirm.

entries.q: Does the system claim a betting edge?

a.answer: No. Every committed analytics artifact carries edge_claimed=false, and against real closing lines the finding is that the market is efficient. This is a calibrated predictor whose honest win is matching the devigged close within noise, plus a measured in-game conditioning improvement -- not a dollar edge. Accuracy is not edge, and an honest reject is treated as a success.

entries.q: How well does the model do against the market's own probabilities?
alt_phrasings: do you beat the market's Brier
is the model sharper than the price

a.answer: It does not beat the market's Brier. The in-game Brier skill score of model versus market is at or below zero everywhere: for MLB all-innings the model Brier is 0.237684 against the market's 0.206653 (skill score -0.1502), and for international soccer all-minutes it is 0.227887 against 0.142726 (skill score -0.5967). Both model and market crush the base-rate baseline, which is expected and is not an edge.

entries.q: What did the full-season backtest actually prove?
alt_phrasings: are you well calibrated but not profitable

a.answer: The full-season leak-free walk-forward backtest (with truncation-invariance proven) shows the model is well-calibrated but does not beat the close: season Brier 0.208 versus the closing line's 0.198. Spread and total pregame closing-line value is essentially zero, with correlation-with-outcome of 0.001. That negative result is exactly what a rigorous validation framework is supposed to produce.

entries.q: What is the one measured win the system does claim?

a.answer: The one measured calibration win is in-game conditioning: fusing the pregame rating prior with the realized mid-game state sharpens the win-probability forecaster, moving Brier from 0.209 to 0.159 for NBA and 0.241 to 0.126 for MLB on real out-of-sample corpora. It is labeled calibration, not a dollar edge, because a live book sees the score too. edge_claimed stays false.

entries.q: What happened in the playoff replay validation?
alt_phrasings: did you have a playoff edge

a.answer: Replaying the Finals games G1 through G3 through the in-game projector produced a pooled win-probability Brier of 0.34 to 0.40 in-series -- worse than a coin flip. That is the cleanest proof in the system that the playoff market is efficient and there is no pregame playoff edge. It is reported as an honest negative result.

entries.q: How was this AI actually built?

a.answer: It is a solo human-architected build over an agentic pipeline: across 3,224 commits from 2026-03-09 to 2026-07-22, about 95.75% are agent-authored and 67.9% carry a Claude co-author trailer. The busiest single day logged 275 commits. The honest framing is one human directing the pipeline and owning the ship/reject and validation decisions, not one person hand-typing thousands of commits.

entries.q: Was this really built over 13 months?
alt_phrasings: how long did the build take

a.answer: No -- an earlier 13-month figure is not supported by git and was dropped. The commit history spans 2026-03-09 to 2026-07-22, roughly four and a half months. The honest description is an intensive solo build across that window.

entries.q: How many fact-claims has the system generated, and how many are actually verified?

a.answer: The claims corpus holds 103,048 generated fact-claims across 103 families; 99 families carry a validation sidecar and 4 do not. Of 101,865 claims sampled for validation, 101,864 verified with 0 mismatches and 1 unverifiable -- covering 98.85% of generated claims. The metadata is explicit that generated outnumbers verified by design, so 'verified' never silently means 'generated'.

entries.q: Did you once claim more verified claims than you could back up?
alt_phrasings: a claim count with no artifact

a.answer: Yes -- an earlier figure of roughly 52,343 verified claims has no surviving artifact and is not claimed. The corpus is now presented as its honest split instead: 103,048 generated fact-claims with a validation sample verifying 101,864 of 101,865 sampled. The generated/validated distinction is stated up front on purpose.

entries.q: Which sports have the most tested hypotheses, and how many held up?

a.answer: By survival rate, NBA leads at 0.56 (42 confirmed of 75 testable), tennis 0.5455, soccer 0.5179, and MLB the lowest at 0.3974. Across all four the overall survival rate is 0.5039 on 256 testable hypotheses. Roughly half surviving is the expected shape when the gate is genuinely trying to refute each candidate.

entries.q: What kinds of effects survive your gate, and which mostly fail?
alt_phrasings: do rest and fatigue signals hold up

a.answer: By category, officiating effects survive best at 0.75 and the small travel bucket at 1.0, while rest-and-fatigue effects survive weakest at just 0.3056 (11 of 36 testable). That is a useful honesty signal: the folk-wisdom rest-and-fatigue story mostly does not replicate under a leak-free gate. Every bucket is reported as-is, with no dollar or edge claim attached.

entries.q: Give me an example of a mechanism that did confirm.

a.answer: The back-to-back rest penalty in NBA confirmed with an effect of -1.73 points of margin (p=0.005645) on a 4,732-row corpus, meaning teams on zero days rest averaged worse margins than those with a day off. Home-court advantage also confirmed at about 3.4 points. The ledger stores each with its p-value and corpus so the number can be reproduced, not taken on faith.

entries.q: Give me an example of a mechanism that came back null.

a.answer: Rest-differential-versus-margin came back null: the correlation between home-minus-away rest and home margin was about -0.018 with p well above any threshold, so no usable effect. A star-injury usage-vacuum event study and pace-mismatch variance also landed null. These sit in the same ledger as the confirms, counted rather than quietly dropped.

entries.q: Do any of your findings flip verdict when you re-test them?

a.answer: Yes, and the system keeps the whole history rather than the flattering last row. Five families are flagged as flipped -- for example NBA three-in-four fatigue went null then confirmed on a larger corpus, and an MLB staff-day-after fatigue chain went null, confirmed, then null again. A positive full-sample lift that sign-flips out of sample is treated as the overfit signature and caught, not published.

entries.q: How many hypotheses has the interaction factory tested?

a.answer: The interaction factory that composes confirmed single-mechanism findings into two-way candidates has adjudicated 1,003 of them: 709 not-testable, 239 null, 38 confirmed, and 17 failed-replication. The large not-testable and null majority is the gate doing its job, not a shortfall. The not-testable rows are untested combinations, evidence for nothing either way.

entries.q: Does the answer engine ever refuse to answer?
alt_phrasings: can the system say no data

a.answer: Yes, refusing is a designed behavior. In a 1,307-question coverage stress test the status split was 399 ok, 560 no_data, 42 not_supported, 181 ambiguous, 125 refused, and 0 errors, for an honest coverage rate of 0.3662 on the questions that expect an answer. A correct no_data or not_supported is scored as a design pass, not a failure -- the engine is fail-closed rather than improvising.

entries.q: What happens when someone asks the system for an edge or ROI?
alt_phrasings: how does it handle profit questions

a.answer: It refuses all of them. In the coverage stress test the edge-language category had 125 questions with an ok-rate of 0.0 -- every single one was refused -- and the prediction-winprob category likewise refused all 85. That refusal is enforced by the no-edge rail, not left to a model's discretion.

entries.q: Is the answer-engine regression bank passing?

a.answer: Yes -- the answer-quality regression bank runs 87 checks and all 87 pass at the FULL tier, with 0 failures. Those are fail-closed status and receipt checks: a correct no_data, not_supported, or ambiguous response counts as a pass. It measures answer consistency, not any edge.

entries.q: Do the public showcase numbers actually reproduce?
alt_phrasings: can I reproduce the site numbers

a.answer: Every showcase builder module carries a self-check, and the latest check-all report shows all of them returning PASS. Separately, the repo's check_all self-check passes 52 of 52 on a bare clone and runs green in public CI, where the trail also preserves the first run that honestly failed 46 of 52 on a path-portability bug before it was fixed. Keeping the red run in the history is the discipline, not an embarrassment.

entries.q: What is the model's prop-stat accuracy, and is it leak-free?
alt_phrasings: how accurate are the player projections

a.answer: On a 20,354-row production-model chronological holdout (last 20% by date, run through the production inference path), the mean absolute errors are PTS 4.83, REB 1.92, AST 1.39, and FG3M 0.89. The verify script fail-closes if any stat drifts more than 0.02 from these. It is leak-free and competitive with published prop-model benchmarks, and this holdout set is the honest lead accuracy claim.

entries.q: What is the win-probability model's headline accuracy?
alt_phrasings: how good is the win probability

a.answer: The five-way NNLS win-probability stack reads 0.709 accuracy and 0.193 Brier under three-fold walk-forward validation. That is a calibration number, reported without any claim that it beats a closing line -- the full-season test shows it does not.

entries.q: Do the computer-vision features add predictive value today?
alt_phrasings: do tracking features help the model

a.answer: Not yet. Every CV-derived feature carries SHAP importance of about 0.0 in the production prop models today, and the CV-lift report reads has_cv_data false. The plumbing is complete and the thesis is credible, but it is honestly labeled as not-yet-a-measured-edge rather than a moat.

entries.q: How many games has the tracking pipeline actually processed?

a.answer: The CV features table holds 17,254 rows across 241 games covering 252 distinct real NBA player IDs, with 29 distinct feature names. The volume is real, but the file itself notes these are coverage stats only -- no accuracy or MOT metric is claimed, because those are not benchmarked against labeled ground truth.

entries.q: How many players does the tracker actually hold per game?
